In the mornings, sunlight streams in through the skylight overhead to bathe the place in warmth, while at sundown, the surrounding forests in Hunter invite you to tee up the outdoor fire pit and take it all in. From $218 per night.

Perks: full-service kitchen, hot tub, BBQ grill

The term “cozy” is often synonymous with “small.” Not so in this jaw-dropping A-frame that sleeps 10 of your luckiest pals. Surrounded by miles of woods, the location sets the stage for a tranquil escape, but those who are looking for a few activities to pass the time will be happy to discover its proximity to the Rockbridge Nature Preserve, as well as local wineries and breweries. While the white shiplap interior, floor-to-ceiling windows, and floating staircase create an airy feel, there’s also plenty of texture among the leather, wood and rattan furnishings to warm things up. From $882 per night.

Perks: rainfall shower, wood-burning fireplace

Visitors to this New England town—known to be one of the best ski areas on the East coast—often come to hit the slopes. But even those who have no interest in venturing outside on a cold winter day will relish their visit if they stay at this Scandinavian-inspired cabin. Light wood beams and moldings, thick rugs underfoot, and minimalist furnishings tempt even the most dedicated skiers to stay indoors. While you’re holed up in your new lodgings, enjoy a blissful soak under the rainfall showerhead or take in the view from the glass wall in the bedroom that offers an unobscured view during leaf-peeping season and beyond. From $545 per night.

Perks: outdoor patio, fully-stocked kitchen, luxury linens

An hour outside Boise, situated among the Rocky Mountains, lies a magical escape where you can leave all your stress on the car ride up. This A-frame cabin features luxury amenities, stylish furniture, and views for days (you can choose whether to enjoy them through the floor-to-ceiling windows or while relaxing in the hot tub on the deck). Don’t sleep on the curb appeal—the asymmetric A-frame structure of the home is only the beginning of your visual journey. Inside, warm wooden walls, one-of-a-kind furniture, an indoor hammock, and a marble-clad shower await. The home is a 30-minute drive from the Mountain Loop Highway, which grants access to outdoor adventures in Big Four Ice Caves, Lake Twenty-Two, Heather Lake, and Gothic Basin, to name a few. Perks: Electric vehicle charging, pontoon style rental, modern open kitchen

When the weather agrees, head down to the lake for a dip. From $287 per night.

#4864. Every Lululemon Shoe Ranked: I Tested Them All, and I Have Thoughts

After putting Lululemon’s full shoe lineup to the test, here’s how each pair ranked.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Lululemon set the bar high for athleisure with its buttery-soft leggings, and continues to deliver on that front. However, since it had always been primarily an athletic wear brand, it wasn’t part of the running shoe or walking shoe conversation. But that changed in 2022 when Lululemon expanded into footwear. Since then, the brand has slowly built a following in that category, too.

I originally tried a pair of Lululemon sneakers a few months ago after reading rave reviews, but quickly stopped wearing them because they felt too snug at my usual size. But I kept seeing positive feedback from other people, making me wonder if I wrote them off too soon. After all, Lululemon is known for careful construction, thoughtful tailoring, and high-quality products.

Like many other shoe brands, each of Lululemon’s sneakers is designed with a specific purpose in mind. The brand’s shoes match Lululemon's overall understated aesthetic. While there are a few bright colors here and there, you also have plenty of neutrals and muted shades to choose from. That alone makes them stand out in a sea of eyeball-searing sneakers.

To see what I was missing beyond looks, I tried each of Lululemon’s athletic shoes—BeyondFeel, Split Shift, Wildfeel, and Chargefeel 3—to see which is the best. And since it’s best to know what you’re getting into before you grab a pair just because it matches your favorite gym outfit, I get into the details about each shoe model below. I was surprised at how wide of a range the brand offers: There’s a Lululemon sneaker for just about anything. Still, one had to come out on top. These are the best Lululemon shoes, ranked, based on months of testing.

The BeyondFeel is the shoe I originally passed on before because it ran snug. So, PSA: Consider sizing up if you prefer a roomy fit or have wide feet. While Lululemon says online that these fit true to size, that wasn't the case for me. Once I went up half a size, I was hooked.

The BeyondFeel is Lululemon's max cushioned shoe, so you can think of it like a Hoka Bondi 9 or On Cloudmonster 3. It's designed for everyday use. Think: running errands, power walking, actual running—it's all comfortable in the BeyondFeel.

I noticed a difference from my daily trainers the second I slipped my feet inside. The best way to describe the feeling is like the first time I put on a pair of Align leggings. I was immediately comfortable, with no chafing, pinching, or any other issues.

This shoe has a nice, roomy toe box, giving your feet plenty of room to swell naturally as you go about your day or rack up the mileage. It also has a stable heel and good grip although, heads up: The shoes may squeak a little when you first wear them inside.

Lululemon designed the BeyondFeel differently for women vs. men, adding an extra 2 millimeters of foam at the forefoot to take some pressure off the knees and hips. I wouldn't wear the BeyondFeel for long runs, though—it doesn't have much energy return, which is that slight bouncy feeling you may get in a shoe. But I was happy to log a few miles in them here and there, along with wearing them for weight training and just running errands. Their stylish look and comfortable feel make them a good choice for nearly everyone.

The Split Shift is Lululemon's neutral everyday running shoe, which is another way of saying it's a good shoe for most runners. The first thing you'll notice is how lightweight the shoe is. At 7.8 ounces, it's not the lightest shoe ever made, but it definitely won't feel like your feet are dragging you down when you're logging higher mileage. This sneaker has an equally breezy upper, giving it an overall airy feel.

I really appreciate the springiness of these shoes. It's not so much that it feels like you're running on mini trampolines, but there's a good energy return here to help propel you forward with each step. That's definitely a noticeable change from the BeyondFeel, which has pretty much no energy return by comparison. There's a gusseted tongue that gently hugs your ankle, along with some extra padding around the ankle that prevents rubbing. The outsole doesn't feel as grippy as the BeyondFeel, but it's a good choice for everyday road running.

My only complaint with the Split Shift is that the toe box runs a little narrow. I'm used to running in shoes with a wide toe box, and the Split Shift's smaller width across the toes means they probably won't be my go-to for everyday miles. Like the BeyondFeel, I'd suggest going up a half size if you like a roomy toe box or have wide feet.

Lululemon's Chargefeel 3 looks different from the brand's other shoes out of the box. It has an hourglass shape, with a narrow middle, more room at the toes, and an exaggerated base at the heel for stability. That shape is intentional, since this shoe is made for cross-training, hybrid, and HIIT workouts. The Chargefeel 3 is on the lighter end of weight for a gym shoe at 8 ounces, and it feels light on your feet. Still, it has everything you want in a shoe you'll be doing cross-training in, like a locked-in feeling in the heel, snug laces, and ability to handle lateral movements.

The grip on this shoe is impressive. I was able to stop cleanly while doing direction-changing indoor sprints at the gym, with no squeaking. The shoe also features a ShiftFoam midsole for a little energy return. Its not nearly as bouncy as the Split Shift, though—but you don't want that in a shoe you'll be doing hybrid workouts in anyway.

The Chargefeel 3 has a 6mm heel-to-toe drop, which may be high for those looking for a neutral strength training shoe, so it might not be ideal for lifting. It’s laser-cut mesh helps tamp down on foot sweat, along with Nulu fabric heel lining to mimic the feel of your favorite leggings.

And if you're looking for a running shoe, scroll up. This is really a gym shoe that you can do a little running in in a pinch—not something you want to do any significant mileage in. And while the Chargefeel 3 made me feel locked-in and secure during gym workouts, it's not so comfortable that I'd wear this shoe outside of exercise. If you're looking for a dedicated hybrid shoe, though, it's worth a look.

Some athletic shoe brands will slap deep lugs on a sneaker and call it a trail shoe without addressing other needs. But it's clear that Lululemon's Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There's a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you're going down. Like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. That wasn't a huge deal on shorter runs, but it started to annoy me on longer runs. Like many others on this list, I'd consider going up a half size.

My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that's pretty common in a trail shoe. (It got better with time and more wear.) It's also worth noting that the Wildfeel isn't the most breathable shoe you'll find, and my socks were a little sweatier than usual because of it. None of these are dealbreakers. But it also meant the Wildfeel was my least favorite shoe in Lululemon's lineup.

To choose the best Lululemon shoes, I put each through regular testing over several months. I used each shoe on a near-daily basis for weeks, making sure to test it for the way it was designed. So, I wore the Wildfeel on trails and the Split Shift on daily training runs. During each testing session, I took notes on the shoe's fit, traction, stability, and overall comfort. From there, I ranked each shoe based on its testing results, along with how well it matched up to their intended use.

The best Lululemon shoe for running depends on the type of running you plan to do. If you’re in search of a neutral everyday trainer, the Split Shift is a good choice. It’s lightweight and slightly bouncy, giving you plenty of support and cushioning over daily miles. The BeyondFeel is another solid option. It’s highly cushioned for maximum comfort, making it a better choice for shorter runs.

The best Lululemon shoe for HIIT workouts is the Chargefeel 3. This sneaker has a unique hourglass shape to create a locked-in feel you’ll appreciate during HIIT workouts, along with a wide base for stability. The shoe’s grip is impressive, allowing you to stop quickly and change directions during indoor workouts.

Lululemon used to offer the Strongfeel shoe for strength training, but it’s been discontinued. Now, the Chargefeel 3 is the best option for many strength training workouts due to its wide base and stable platform. But as noted above, the shoe has a higher heel-to-toe drop of 6mm, so it’s not ideal for moves like deadlifts. So if lifting is your priority, you might want to consider a more neutral shoe for optimal biomechanics.

Lululemon often says online that its shoes fit true to size, but that wasn't my experience. I don't have wide feet, but I do appreciate a roomy toe box to accommodate the natural foot swelling that happens on workouts and runs. Most Lululemon shoes tend to run narrow across the toe box. If you have wide feet or just prefer more room to spread your toes, consider going up a size.

#4863. Attention All Humans: AI Is Like a Spy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Do you remember when it would take a minute or two for a website to fully load? The picture would reveal itself in incremental pixels until you could finally view it in its entirety. It was the era of banner ads and pop-ups, a rudimentary transference of billboard marketing to the World Wide Web.

Later, algorithms scanned, then shaped, our behavioral and consumption patterns. The length of time a user watched a video or stopped scrolling to “read more” became the metric for advertising effectiveness. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technology measures how you behave online, like a little spy watching your every move without your noticing.

Welcome to the attention economy. “Pay attention!” the internet demands. “Or at least get paid for it,” advertising executives suggest. That is what influencer marketing is all about. The more clicks, the more views, the more money flows.

Joe Marchese and Jonathan Bing have penned a new book, Human Dot AI, that chronicles the rise of advertising from the era of Mad Men advertisers on Madison Avenue to today. Both authors have extensive experience in the industry themselves. Marchese is an entrepreneur and media executive, CEO of Human Ventures Holdings, co-founder of Casa Komos Brands Group, and chairman of Groundswell. He previously founded true[X] and led advertising revenue at Fox Networks Group. Bing is a marketing and communications executive who has held leadership roles at Netflix, 21st Century Fox, and Vice. He is also a journalist who has written for The New York Times, Los Angeles Times, and Wired. The authors wish to help readers reclaim their attention or, in their words, to “restore a sense of agency, choice, and control over the time and attention that algorithms are not designed to give you.”

Do you remember the ads “Have a Coke and a smile” or “I’d like to teach the world to sing in perfect harmony”? They lent viewers a sense of community and connection through catchy slogans and jingles that captured our collective imagination. Watching television, in a sense, was a shared experience. No fast-forwarding through commercials, no pre-recording to watch your favorite show at a later time. The Super Bowl remains an exception as one of the most popular live televised sports events of the year in which the legendary commercials running at roughly $10 million per 30-second slot are often as memorable as the game itself. According to Nielsen, a global leader in measuring audience behavior, however, nearly half of all TV viewers have switched to streaming services such as Netflix and YouTube. In a recent video call, Marchese admitted that consuming social media today "is like watching television," but not in the same way we used to in the pre-Internet era. Today, asynchronous viewing has made watching programs a much more isolating experience.

With 5.8 billion mobile phone users worldwide, 70 percent of the planet’s population has a robust digital communications-based lifestyle. Marchese and Bing aim to offer a way back to human connection despite our AI-saturated lives. Around the time that Facebook’s News Feed feature was launched (yes, there was a time when you actually had to actively look for people by clicking on various profiles), it stopped being a place to connect and became more a place to advertise, albeit subtly. Advertising became adjacent to social activity itself, deeply embedded in the content without our realizing it. Consumer engagement became the name of the game. No more annoying pop-up ads. Enter the gamification of social media consumption. We are no longer simply consuming information (and patiently waiting for pictures to load); we are now participating in a game designed to capture and retain our attention—all day long. As a result, two problems have emerged: the lack of editorial supervision and the machines’ lack of understanding humans. Content is no longer about bringing people together but, rather, about keeping people engaged and enraged.

“[N]o algorithm can replace what happens when people come together around something real—a shared experience, story, or glass” (Marchese & Bing, 2026). An automated, algorithm-driven life flattens intimacy, commercializes our need for connection, and monetizes our very human desire to love and be loved. How we spend our time and attention truly matters. These resources are finite, but an algorithm doesn’t care why a user is engaged with the content. It is designed to feed us more of the same.

Digital hygiene is key to maintaining a sense of equilibrium in our tech-driven lives. Attention-grabbing is as old as the advertising industry itself. From the town crier to our social media apps, brands yearn for our attention. But in the end, we, as humans, get to decide if we give it or not.

Marchese, J., & Bing, J. (2026). Human Dot AI: How the Fight for Your Attention Became the World’s Biggest Business. AMPLIFY PUBLISHING.

#4862. The 7 Best Head Shavers for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Get the chrome dome of your dreams with these scalp shavers.

AS MEN, THE decision to go bald isn’t always one that’s made for us (thanks, genetics). But how you deal with hair loss is entirely in your hands. Sure, there are some viable hair loss treatments and shampoos for thinning hair that we certainly back. For many men, it's easier to just bite the bullet and shave their hair completely to offset any future thinning woes. If you are one of these men, more power to you! Hell, some men do it even if they’re not experiencing hair loss—and that’s cool, too. Investing in a quality head shaver will double down on the convenience factor of being bald by making the entire process seamless.

When you do choose to shave your head, the tools you use to do it are paramount. That’s where the best head shavers come in. These high-tech gadgets are specifically designed to make shaving your head easier, whether it’s through a multi-head ergonomic design or close-cutting technology (or both).

Far easier than heading to the barbershop every few days, these electric shavers are meant to be used at home. Think of them as an easier, safer, and quicker alternative to carefully taking a razor to your dome. But before investing in a shaver, there are a few key factors to keep in mind to ensure you select the absolute best one for you.

This tiny but powerful shaver is designed to give your scalp the closest shave possible, whether you prefer to do it dry, wet, or with the aid of other products. The five ScalpSafe shaving heads wrap around the curves of your head for a microscopically close shave, and the additional attachments, like a pre-shave exfoliation brush and precision trimmer, are nice bonuses.

Our editors also love that it pairs nicely with our favorite shaving creams and pre-shave oils, in case you want an even deeper cut. Its portable design makes it easy to carry in your luggage, though its travel case is sold separately. Not to mention, the five heads of this shaver definitely give an incredibly close shave—as close as the Remington and the Braun, both of which we found to be top of the heap in our testing process.

We also appreciate the additional attachments that this one comes with, unlike the Remington, particularly the pre-shave exfoliating brush, which not only helps give a closer shave, but also feels pretty damn good on your dome (you’ll want to only use this if you have a tiny bit of stubble though—the bristles aren’t long enough to reach through longer hair).

In theory, the trimmer attachment and the accompanying guards are great if you want to trim your beard (the brand also says you can use it to trim your body and other areas), but we found that the design of the device makes that difficult. Since it’s meant to be held in the palm of your hand, it’s not as easy to use on your face as a more traditional razor design like the Braun or even the Andis. We would probably skip that and relegate this device to only our heads, which, at a comparable price point to other models like the Remington, is OK.

Read More: How to Give Yourself a Buzzcut

If you’re in a rush, this easy-to-use shaver may be your answer. Thanks to the pivoting shaver heads that hug each curve of your head, the brand says that this device can shave your entire head in just two minutes.

After testing the Remington Balder Pro for over a year, we can safely say that it easily gave us a head shave in less than five minutes, which is great for guys who cut their dome weekly. We love the hair capture chamber, which collects hair for easy cleanup, and its non-slip grip gives you extra control when you're mowing through your head.

Keep in mind that this is designed only for head shaving, so if you’re looking for a more multi-purpose solution, you’ll want to go with a more traditional electric shaver like the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus. And since there aren’t any additional attachments like the kind that come with others, like the Freebird, you’re really only going to use this to give your head a smooth, clean shave (which it is frankly very good at doing).

The price is comparable to other head shavers, but we found that the performance outmatches them, so it’s a great investment if you’re a guy who shaves his head often and doesn’t mind having a separate tool just for that task.

If you’re not the smooth-shave type, but still want to give yourself a close buzz without heading to the barber, the Shortcut Pro delivers. With multiple length options via interchangeable combs, this shaver allows you to try different buzz looks on your own.

As the product image suggests, the Shortcut Pro is super compact, which makes it great for tossing in a Dopp kit and taking on trips. The feel of the shaver takes a second to get used to, but once you learn how to wield it, you'll find it does a solid job of staying cut-free while providing a solid shave.

It’s worth repeating that this won’t give you a close, clean shave, but it is handy if you like more of a stubble look. The design isn’t perfect and is less ergonomic than the Remington or one of the similarly designed shavers, but once you get the hang of it, it’s pretty foolproof.

Our one gripe is that because of the curved design, which is nice for hugging the shape of your head, it’s a bit difficult for detailed work around your ears or cleaning up your neck. A more traditional clipper is better for those things, but that’s a small price to pay for the convenience this one offers.

Like Braun’s previous versions, the Series 9 Pro+ has proven to be effective in performance. Not only is it one of our favorite head shavers, but it’s seen as the “Rolls-Royce of shaving instruments” by Faheem Alexander, barber and owner of Faheem's Hands of Precision in Philadelphia.“I highly recommend [it] because of the unparalleled ease and comfort it provides while also ensuring a super close shave,” he says. “The accompanying portable charging case makes this super easy to throw in a bag and get numerous weeks of shaves without plugging it in.”

During our trial run, we found out that the fast-speed device can cut up to 40,000 cuts per minute. Thanks to its waterproof capability, you can use it in the shower for a refreshing shaving experience. We also love that the device comes with a SmartCare center, which maintains the quality for longer use and makes cleaning up a breeze.

While this isn’t technically a head shaver in the way the two Remingtons or Freebird are, we found in our testing that it performs just as well at shaving your head as it does at shaving your face—it is our best electric razor.

What that means to us is that if you’re looking to streamline the number of devices you have in your arsenal, but don’t want to sacrifice power or efficacy, this is an ideal option. It’s expensive—as the Rolls-Royce of shaving instruments is expected to be—but if you’re using it for multiple things like shaving your head and face, that helps justify the cost a bit more.

Ever wonder how your barber gets such a close shave when he’s doing skin fades or cleaning up your neck? Enter this foil shaver, which is hard to beat when it comes to closeness. Not to mention, it’s a go-to for plenty of barbers. Speaking of which, Alexander gives the Andis tool his stamp of approval because it works efficiently for shaving experiences at home and in the barbershop.

It operates well on battery, delivering up to 80 minutes of run time on a single charge—a duration that’s twice as long as others on this list. The price point may be higher than most on this list, but the results make up for the difference.

This is definitely a classic for a reason—it really gets the job done with an incredibly smooth shave. However, it’s aggressive and not the gentlest experience, especially if you’re just beginning with it. Theoretically, you can use this on your face and other areas, too, but we found that the shaving experience is too harsh for us to use anywhere but our head and neck. You’ll also likely want to finish with some sort of lotion or moisturizer to minimize potential irritation.

Manscaped is one of the most consistent brands in men’s grooming, and this head shaver is a perfect example of why. It simply gets the basics right for a more enjoyable, less irritating shave. The grip, which invites palming, is super user-friendly, making moving the blades along your head easy with minimal effort (or risk of dropping it).

The brand’s signature SkinSafe blade guards make cuts and nicks rare, while the magnetic connection makes clean-up and replacements easy. With a 9,500 RPM motor, it shaves smoothly and efficiently. We found it also required minimal passes to get a full shave. Adding to its user-friendliness, the Dome Shaver Pro battery lasts up to 90 minutes and is USB-C chargeable. Plus, it’s waterproof and includes a sturdy hard-shell travel case.

This head shaver from the always reliable Philips Norelco is a great choice if you’re looking for a smooth, comfortable shave without the hassle. Its 360-degree flexing head follows the contours of your scalp, while the 36 self-sharpening ComfortCut blades deliver an even shave without putting unnecessary pressure on your skin.

The ergonomic grip makes it easy to maneuver, while the PowerAdapt Sensor automatically adjusts power to match hair density as you go. With up to 90 minutes of cordless use, water resistance, and a convenient travel case, it’s a reliable option for both everyday grooming and travel.

Most head shavers feature multiple razor heads to help hug the contours of your head so you can easily navigate areas that are hard to see. The multiple razor heads can also help limit cuts, as the design adjusts to curved angles much better than a single, straight razor.

For the quickest, most adaptable (read: lowest maintenance) shaving experience, look for devices with shaving heads in the five-to-seven range, like the Freebird FlexSeries or Remington Balder Pro. That being said, don’t fall into the common trap of thinking that more shaving heads automatically equals a more powerful shave, as the Braun Series 9 Pro Plus is one of the most powerful options on the market and only has four shaving blades.

Most head shavers on this list can be used dry, which means as long as your hair is already short enough (no more than a couple of days of growth), you can shave with no moisture or product. What's also great is that some options are waterproof, making your shaving experience in the shower a total breeze and easy to clean up.

Plus, you can use most wet/dry shavers with shaving products, so if you prefer to begin with a pre-shave oil to protect your scalp and then add a shaving cream or lotion to help with gliding. Follow it up by rinsing the product off your head—just make sure to also clean any leftover product from the razor heads before you put it away. However, there are a couple of options we recommend that do not have this capability, so if you’re a dedicated shower shaver, focus solely on the wet/dry devices.

A good cordless head shaver can last as long as 90 minutes, which means you can go a whole week without charging the battery. They also unlock the ability to shave in the shower or on the road without having to be plugged in. If you're constantly on the move and shave your head regularly, you will find that cordless options offer lots of convenience and save even more time.

Even before joining the bald brotherhood, most of us have all had an electric razor or beard trimmer die out before we've finished the job. Nobody wants to sport a half-trimmed beard or uneven body hair, but the absolute last spot you'll want an uneven shave is on your dome, as it's the hardest to hide.

To avoid walking around with a patchy skull, keep battery life in mind when choosing an electric shaver. Consider how long you typically take to shave your entire head—and how often you tend to charge devices—before finalizing your decision.

The first question to ask is: Does this shaver come with a case included? If yes, then you're going to want to look at what type of case it is. For frequent travelers, a carrying case made to fit neatly in a Dopp kit or luggage should be a priority. However, if you're just looking for something to store it in, you can allow for more size, given that it'll more easily hold every attachment or replacement piece, so there won't be any long search involved when needed.

For the past four years, Men's Health's grooming writers and editors have tested over 15 head shavers to determine the best-performing options for men. We also spoke with the barber and owner of Faheem’s Hands of Precision in Philadelphia, Faheem Alexander, who has put dozens of top-selling head shavers to the test and evaluated their effectiveness, durability, and ease of use.

In addition to all of this expertise and hands-on experience, we researched and dug into the top head shavers on the market to determine which to test. Following that extensive research and testing process, we landed on these seven best head shavers for men.

#4861. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Lung Cancer Can Look Like Anyone

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Picture someone with lung cancer. Now picture a 24-year-old soccer player in the prime of his life. A filmmaker in her early 40s with a camera in her hand, doing what she loves best. A busy mom of two, with a shoulder so sore she can’t pick up her newborn, yet struggling to get a diagnosis.

The gap between the picture in our heads and the people actually being diagnosed is costing time. And time is the one thing with lung cancer you cannot get back.

We know that lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide and the leading cause of cancer death. And while lung cancer incidence rates are falling in many countries as fewer people smoke, lung cancer in people who have never smoked is on the rise globally, both as a proportion and in absolute numbers.

According to the CDC, as many as 20% of lung cancers diagnosed in the US are in people who have never smoked. Data suggests that non-smoking lung cancer is now among the most common causes of cancer-related deaths worldwide.

The numbers are stark. Lung cancer can affect anyone. And that includes the young – like Alex, one of the subjects of a powerful new short documentary commissioned by the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK for their Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign.

Alex was a 24-year-old soccer player who died just weeks after receiving a diagnosis of Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) positive lung cancer, following several misdiagnoses born of the fact that no one suspected lung cancer in one so young, fit, and with no smoking history. The film was made by filmmaker Sarah Li, who herself was diagnosed with Stage 4 EGFR+ lung cancer in April 2024, just a month after Alex died from the same mutation of the disease, and charts her journey with survivor’s guilt, what an earlier diagnosis may have meant for Alex, and what that fact means for her own future.

Ahead of Lung Cancer Awareness Month in November, I sat down with my friend, Gini Harrison, to talk about the film, her own journey, and why catching lung cancer sooner matters so much. Gini is a Professor of Psychology at The Open University, a trustee of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK, and is living with stage 4 EGFR-positive lung cancer. She’s also the mom at the top of this piece, whose sore shoulder was initially attributed to breastfeeding posture.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

Gini Harrison: I’d had my son, Michael, in February 2021 and was on maternity leave. My daughter, Emily, was five. I think the shoulder pain started around March, but that was it. No cough, no breathlessness… nothing that made me think about my lungs.

Initially, they gave me painkillers, which helped a bit. But the pain kept getting worse. Eventually, I started losing movement and strength in my arm, and it got to the point where I couldn’t pick up my son anymore.

This was all happening during COVID, so my appointments were over the telephone. Eventually, after months without being examined face-to-face, I paid to see a shoulder specialist. As soon as he touched my shoulder blade and I practically leaped out of the chair, he knew something wasn’t right. He ordered an MRI, which showed a tumor in my shoulder blade and another in my upper right lung. In December 2021, I was diagnosed with stage IV lung cancer.

Gini Harrison: I wasn’t thinking, “This must be cancer.” I was just thinking, “Why isn’t this getting better?”

And I think that distinction matters. Patients shouldn’t have to identify their own disease before they can get help. You should be able to say that something is wrong and be listened to.

Gini Harrison: It was devastating. So many of my first questions were about the children: “How are we going to tell them?” “Am I going to be here to see them grow up?” “Will they remember me?” Suddenly, there was a question mark over a future I’d taken for granted.

I was also completely shocked by the type of cancer. If someone had said breast cancer, I don’t think I would have been anywhere near as surprised. But lung cancer?! I’d always associated it with smoking, and I’d never smoked.

I hadn’t imagined that this particular cancer could ever happen to me. So yes, I had some assumptions that I now challenge. I understand how deeply rooted they are because I had them too.

Gini Harrison: People are often shocked, and one of the first questions is whether I smoked.

And they often look healthy. That doesn’t mean everything is easy, or that there aren’t side effects. It just means you can’t tell what someone is dealing with by looking at them.

I think we’ve given lung cancer such a narrow public image that people outside it can become almost invisible.

Gini Harrison: Oh, yes! Once, I spoke to a doctor about a breathing problem after radiotherapy. He asked, “How much did you smoke?” When I said I’d never smoked, he replied, “Well, how did you get lung cancer then?”

On another occasion, I went to a hospice for help managing side effects, and someone there asked, “How are you still alive?” That’s quite a thing to hear when you’ve come looking for support!

When people ask about smoking, I try to explain that I’ve never smoked and I’m certainly not alone. Never smoking doesn’t make you immune. But I’m also very clear that nobody deserves lung cancer, whether they’ve smoked or not. We shouldn’t be creating a hierarchy of who deserves compassion.

Smoking history matters medically. But in a personal conversation, “How are you doing?” is a much kinder place to start.

Gini Harrison: Lung cancer isn’t one single disease. Two people can both have lung cancer, but different changes in their cells may be driving it.

Genes contain the instructions that tell our cells how to work, including when to grow and divide. Changes in those genes (called mutations) can cause cells to keep dividing when they shouldn’t, forming a tumor. In my case, there’s a mutation in a gene called EGFR.

EGFR-positive lung cancer is a type of non-small cell lung cancer caused by a genetic mutation in the EGFR gene, which keeps the EGFR receptor switched “on,” leading to uncontrolled cell growth and enhanced cancer cell survival.

Biomarker testing looks for these changes, as well as other features of the cancer that can guide treatment. If we know what’s helping the cancer grow, there may be a medication that specifically targets it.

The word “genetic” can sound scary, particularly when you have children. But these changes usually develop in cancer cells over a person’s lifetime. They aren’t necessarily inherited.

Gini Harrison: Please get it checked. And if it persists, worsens or doesn’t improve with treatment, go back. Explain what’s changed and how it’s affecting your life. Ask, “What happens next if this doesn’t get better?”

The symptoms don’t always look like lung symptoms. Mine was shoulder pain.

Most symptoms will turn out to be something other than cancer. But when a symptom continues to worsen, the original explanation needs to be reconsidered. Lower risk doesn’t mean no risk.

And I don’t want all the responsibility to fall on patients to keep pushing. Reassurance should come with a next step.

Gini Harrison: Once I had recovered from my initial treatment, I realized that I wanted to help others in my situation, so I became a trustee of the charity EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK. Through this work, we produced a film, Our Lungs: Time to Breathe. At the heart of it, it challenges the perception of what someone with lung cancer looks like.

The hardest part is how close to home it feels. Alex was so young, and that worked against him. Watching his family talk about what happened is heartbreaking. It’s just so unfair.

Gini Harrison: Sarah’s story shows life continuing alongside lung cancer. She’s a filmmaker with ambitions, people she loves, and things she wants to do.

Through Alex’s family, you see the enormity of the loss. I hope people feel that, rather than simply hearing another statistic.

Gini Harrison: For me, the biggest thing is that my children are growing up and I’m here to see it. Michael is now five (the age Emily was when I was diagnosed), and Emily is about to turn ten. I can’t tell you how grateful I am to be here with them.

It wasn’t about big bucket-list things. It was about being here every day. Seeing Michael start school. Seeing Emily reach double figures. Those milestones are enormous when you’ve wondered whether you’d get to see them.

After chemotherapy and radiotherapy, I’ve had no evidence of disease since May 2022, and my scans remain stable. But a big change has been seeing the progress in available treatment. It gives me more hope about what might be available if I need treatment again.

The public image of lung cancer still needs to catch up. We need better recognition of symptoms, access to appropriate testing and treatment, and support for the whole person. As a psychologist as well as a patient, I’m particularly aware that psychological well-being and family life need attention alongside the cancer itself.

Gini Harrison: I’d love for people to share the film and help get it in front of those who wouldn’t normally think lung cancer has anything to do with them. And take something from it into everyday life: book the appointment you’ve been putting off, ask your doctor about testing, or respond with kindness when someone tells you about their diagnosis.

Just being willing to rethink your assumptions could make a difference.

Gini Harrison: “You don’t have to put a brave face on with me. How are you really doing?”

When you look well, or your scans are good, people can assume you’re “fine now”. But I’m not sure the fear ever completely goes away. Every scan is terrifying. It feels like there’s a sword of Damocles hanging over my head, and part of me is waiting for the bad scan. I also still have lasting side effects from treatment, and probably always will.

My life has fundamentally changed. Some of that has brought good things, but it doesn’t make the difficult parts disappear. It helps when someone gives you room to be honest about both, without expecting you to reassure them or turn everything into a positive story.

Gini and I have been friends for nearly 30 years, and, while she’d probably cringe to hear me say it, I remain in awe of the way she approaches life with cancer. I am so grateful for her sharing her experiences with me for this column. What Gini asks of us is simple: look again, ask the question, listen, and act on your instincts. Our Lungs: Time to Breathe is where that starts for her. You can learn more about the Our Lungs: Time to Breathe campaign and the wider work of EGFR Positive Lung Cancer UK by clicking the links. — Robin Hough

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4860. Beware of Rehab Recruitment Scams

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Imagine you’ve been struggling with alcohol addiction. Every waking moment is spent either drinking or thinking about drinking. You don’t even want to drink anymore, but you just keep doing it. In a rare moment of lucidity, you decide it’s time to get help. This opportunity for help may come only once. Your life depends on getting genuine help right now.

But what if the person who answers the phone when you call is a salesperson, not a qualified admissions agent, and gets paid for every person they send to a specific program? What if the center offering the highest kickback this month provides a low quality of care or cuts you loose too soon? What if your family has spent their life savings to get you this care?

Situations like this are troublingly common. What’s behind them, and how can patients and their families avoid being scammed?

The following composite scenario lays out many of the practices involved in this kind of impersonation and the patient brokering that often follows.

A woman—we’ll call her Melissa—decides to seek help for opioid addiction. She googles a trusted treatment center in her town—we’ll call it Hometown Recovery—and dials the number that appears at the top of the page.

When an agent answers, Melissa breathes a sigh of relief. She believes she’s talking with someone at Hometown. The agent neither confirms nor denies Melissa’s assumption and asks what kind of insurance she has. If Melissa had Medicaid, that would likely be the end of the call. If she had private insurance, the agent would recommend a specific program “based on her insurance.”

But let’s say Melissa doesn’t have insurance at all. The agent offers to get insurance for her, for free. Melissa suspects something is off. She asks, “Is this Hometown Recovery?” The agent says, “We work with them. I can get you there,” and keeps asking questions. Melissa presses, and after she asks several times, the exasperated agent says, “Yes.”

Melissa accepts the offer for free insurance and is admitted to a program 600 miles away. She’s on a plane the next day and arrives just as withdrawal symptoms begin. She enters the center’s detox unit immediately.

In four days, she is thinking a little clearer. She wonders how she ended up here when she wanted to go to Hometown Recovery. She begins asking questions and ultimately says she wants to leave. Staff members respond that she needs to stay in detox for seven days because that’s what her insurance specified.

She agrees to stay, and at the end of seven days, she enters the center’s primary treatment program. She’s three weeks into residential care when the insurance company realizes her policy is fraudulent and cancels it. The profit-driven treatment center terminates her care. Melissa is far from home with no money, nowhere to go, and no way to get home.

Meanwhile, Hometown Recovery never heard from her. If Melissa has relatives back home who can help, she may be able to get there. But if—like so many people with her circumstances—she doesn’t have anyone, she is now homeless in a strange city after receiving partial treatment.

She took the brave step of asking for help, and she’s been robbed of an opportunity to heal. The call center hijacked her recovery, and this could prove fatal for Melissa.

Impersonation, in the business sense, involves one entity advertising or presenting as another. It’s often a way for unscrupulous businesses to capitalize on the good reputation of more established ones. In the treatment world, some independent or treatment-center-owned call centers buy ads using other centers’ exact names.

When Melissa googled her local treatment center, she saw an ad that read, “Hometown Recovery? Call Us Now!” But the call center she reached had purchased ads featuring “Hometown Recovery” as a keyword. This is an impersonation scam, and it’s illegal.

Perhaps worse than ad scams, some call centers impersonate free addiction helplines—someone trustworthy to talk to, confide in. And, like the search ad scammers, they recruit vulnerable people, either into the facility that operates the call center or the one paying the highest kickback. If you’re starting to feel as though these call centers are treating humans as a commodity, you’re not alone.

It’s truly appalling, but patient brokering (or body brokering) is when agencies or individuals receive kickbacks for funneling patients to specific treatment centers. So, instead of a person whose life is at stake being matched to the program that can best care for them, they’re turned over to the highest bidder.

Call centers are one patient brokering channel. But even police, people working in recovery, or those involved in meeting-based programs may receive kickbacks for recruitment. Likewise, some people who do street outreach—even very publicly on social media—are paid by treatment centers to bring in patients. Social media itself and websites disguised as general help are also common brokering channels.

Whether and how an influencer, agency, or trusted professional partners with those centers is scrutinized by a complex network of laws and regulations.

What happened to Melissa likely violated several federal laws and regulations, as well as some state statutes, depending upon jurisdiction. And as you might expect, the most meticulous impersonators and brokers will operate in places where state laws are more favorable, or enforcement is low.

Federally, FTC truth-in-advertising laws apply to impersonation, and health care fraud statutes are commonly used to prosecute brokering. Both practices are getting more attention recently at the state level as well, and brokering is now a felony in a few states, including North Carolina, Florida, and Arizona.

With sentences ranging from probation to four years at the high end, it’s clear that brokering laws don’t have the teeth that they should, which is possibly one reason prosecutors seem to prefer fraud charges. Given the danger it can place vulnerable people in, including some documented cases of overdose death following brokered placements, consequences are insufficient to say the least. Some advocates and survivors make a compelling argument that brokering is indistinguishable from human trafficking.

With brokers potentially lurking everywhere, they may feel impossible to avoid. And the last thing we want to do is make patients or their families feel wary of every encounter—not trusting the whole industry could present a major barrier to receiving deeply needed care.

There are a few simple ways to spot scammers and brokers:

Report anything suspicious to the FTC and your state attorney general. Additionally, watch for the following red flags:

When you (or a loved one) reach out for help, the person receiving that call should always treat it as the only chance to save your life. The inhumanity of recovery impersonation scamming and patient brokering is hard to comprehend, but our hope is that knowing a bit about these practices will help you find the right treatment path.

#4859. Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank Review: A Fitness Editor’s Honest Thoughts

I’ve worn this top on runs, at the gym, and beyond.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a fitness editor, I’ve racked up quite the collection of built-in-bra tanks and sports bras for working out. And while they all do their job, there’s one that I love more than the others: my Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank. The main reason? It’s versatile—but also because it’s incredibly stylish and flattering.

I am a big believer in the bra-top combo. It’s way easier to slide on something with a built-in bra and go (and it even helps reduce my ever-growing pile of laundry). But, over the past year, this one has outperformed all the rest and become my go-to top for all kinds of workouts. Whether I’m heading to barre, getting ready to lift, or lacing up my sneakers for a run, I know this top will do exactly what I need it to.

I’ve worn the Super Sleek Bra Tank in quite a few contexts: to the gym, to different types of workout classes, to physical therapy, and even while running. It’s also cute enough and offers enough coverage to wear around town running errands, but I tend to reserve it for working out.

While I wouldn’t usually trust something with a built-in bra on its own for higher-impact workouts, the Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank can handle it. Trust me, I’ve worn it for a 10K race. It’s got enough compression and support to get me through the miles. To be fair, I don’t have the highest demand when it comes to sports bras (if you know what I mean), but thanks to the support features, I think quite a few chest sizes could wear this as a standalone bra-tank combo.

When it comes to other kinds of workouts (like a high-energy class or lifting on my own), the high-compression fabric moves with me through every twist and bend, offering the right balance of stretch and support. It also stays put and requires minimal adjusting after big movements, if at all.

This top is made with Alo’s signature Airlift material, which is made from a sleek blend of durable polyester and stretchy elastane—aka it offers high compression with just enough stretch. Compared to that super soft material you might get in a comfy yoga pant, this top feels more like what you’d get in a classic athletic compression short. It’s a bit thicker, slicker—and it is opaque, so you can feel comfortable wearing it around in public.

The compressive material is also why the top is so supportive. It fits snugly to the body, keeping everything locked in place, while also managing to not feel restrictive or too tight. It also has removable pads (which I lost in the washing machine months ago!), but I’ve found that I don’t need them because the material is so snug. To note: Because it has a tighter fit, the brand recommends that you size up if you have a bigger cup size. (My usual size worked just fine for me.)

Part of the reason I wore this for my 10K race was simply that it looks better on me than just about every other workout tank I own. I think that’s mostly thanks to the compression of the garment, which gives it a smoothing effect and helps make me look snatched.

It has a low scoop neck cut with a racerback silhouette. The longline fit hits a bit lower on your torso than a regular bra would, giving it the look of a cropped tank with the fit of a supportive bra. I love that I can throw this on without worrying about an extra layer and feel a little more covered up than when I head to the gym in a regular sports bra. That said, sometimes I wish it were a bit longer, but most of my workout bottoms are high-waisted, so it ends up feeling long enough.

If you are looking for a bra-tank combo, the Alo Super Sleek Bra Tank is just about the top of the line. The garment’s high-compression, stretchy fit is perfect for a wide range of activities, while still staying comfortable and looking cute. My next move? Buying this top in every color.

#4858. 9 Best Duvet Covers: Editor Sets to Style a Bedscape (2026)

Besides pieces like quilts and coverlets, I always say duvet covers are the best accessories to give a bedscape a bit more personality. Take it from Ariel Kaye, founder of juggernaut bedding brand Parachute, who has filled her eclectic LA home with a range of duvet covers that span vibrant, breezy linens to neutral, crisp percales.

To truly find the best of the best, I rounded up a group of writers and editors to test duvet covers from our favorite bedding brands—featuring muted, structured covers for minimalists and trendy colorways and patterns for maximalists. As for our top pick, we went with Boll & Branch’s Signature Hemmed Duvet Set since it’s organic, has a smooth and breathable feel, and comes in tons of prints and colors for easy styling.

If you’re still on the fence about what to go with for your bedroom, I also tapped AD PRO Directory designers to share what they look for in duvet covers, including materiality and design. Read below to create your dream bedscape this season.

For consistency, all prices listed reflect queen-size duvets unless otherwise noted, but up to king sizes are available for purchase from each brand.

Boll & Branch is one of AD’s favorite brands when it comes to bedding. With super soft sheets and other products made from 100% organic cotton, they have a heavy focus on sustainability and directly sourcing raw materials. The duvet cover follows suit, with long-staple cotton making for a durable piece of bedding that I’ve found is breathable enough for both hot and cold nights.

This organic-cotton duvet set can please pretty much anyone with a traditional bedroom. It has a tried-and-true cotton sateen material that gets softer with every wash, and designs—including subtle botanical prints—that are a must for anyone with classic taste. The earthy tones are great for a grounded bedroom too.

Bring the outdoors in with your styling by pairing one of Boll & Branch’s botanical prints with a textured linen sheet set.

Shop AD editors have stood behind Boll & Branch for years because of the brand’s sustainable business model and high-quality bedding. The signature cotton sheets have even earned a top spot in our best-of guides for the last five years. Just like these sheets, shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher tells me that this Boll & Branch duvet cover’s sateen weave has a buttery soft texture. “The cotton is very smooth, and I maintained a comfortable temperature throughout the night even when bundled up underneath all my bedding,” she says. As a cold sleeper, Arzbeacher loves layering extra throws and blankets on top of her duvet, and she says this ultra-breathable material has all the “cuddly qualities” you’d want without making you overheat. Even better, the bedding is 100% organic, so you can rest knowing you’re not breathing in any harmful chemicals.

This sateen duvet cover also has a zipper closure, so it’s a lot easier for Arzbaecher to slip her Company Store down insert on and off than other button-closure covers she’s tried. “Their solid color range has a lovely mix of earthy hues, and the brand has been releasing more and more patterns, from stripes to florals,” for styling a bed, she adds.

I’m not sure what’s left to say about this bedding brand that hasn’t already been plastered across subway ads or Instagram feeds, but in short, Brooklinen is somewhat of a bedding celebrity. It has garnered cool-kid status by offering top-quality products using Oeko-Tex-certified products at reasonable prices.

The Classic Duvet Cover is made of percale, which can be compared to a crisp cotton button-down shirt. It’s soft and sophisticated in a matte, buttery finish that can be attributed to long-staple cotton fibers that are spun to make stronger but finer yarn.

We are not only big fans of Brooklinen products for their breathable, sustainable materials but also for their versatile designs. With 20 earthy tones, I recommend this duvet cover for any type of bedroom style—but I’d lean towards purchasing for a coastal design because of the soothing colors and prints.

Like Alpert, who has this duvet cover in her bedroom, I recommend styling it with textured linen sheets for a contrasting yet comfortable fabric combination and a throw blanket in complementary neutral and oceanic hues.

Not one but two AD writers love this Brooklinen cotton duvet cover all year long. Shopping writer Julia Harrison calls this super, super soft and very cool to the touch. “It stays cool even when I’ve wrapped myself all the way in it like a caterpillar so I’m never overheating, but I am staying comfy and warm,” she shares. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert says this is her favorite duvet cover of all time, hands-down, because of its unmatched airy and parachute-like quality. “The percale duvet cover has this smooth feel but at the same time it is remarkably light and crisp,” she says. “Apparently, it’s all because of the high-quality single-ply yarns, which are made from strong, long-staple cotton fibers that give it that buttery touch.”

The style potential is a plus here too. Alpert loves the “oyster” print since it strays away from more expected patterns like stripes filling up her linen closet. She got the matching sheets in the same print for this exact reason, saying the swirls remind her of “Hokusai’s waves and stand out in the sea of florals and plaids” in her linen closet.

From pajamas to sheets, Cozy Earth is a favorite of ours—and Oprah thanks to frequent appearances in her Favorite Things lists—for cooling bedding made of bamboo fabric. Its offerings also ring in at a budget-friendly price (especially with the brand’s frequent sales).

Many of the colors in Cozy Earth’s collection are grounded in the earth (to be expected). With this in mind, I see this duvet cover in a minimalist, bohemian, or coastal bedroom. Alpert’s peony pick is just as nice for a romantic bedroom or something seasonal for summer.

The delicate nature of the bedding (both in texture and color) makes it a striking contrast against crisp, patterned accents, like a percale floral sheet set.

When I asked Alpert what her favorite qualities are about Cozy Earth’s signature, silky duvet cover, there were almost too many to count. “This duvet cover is a trifecta of perks: It looks good, feels good, and won’t slip off the comforter,” she says. “But if I had to pick one, I’d say that I love the delicate pink hue and the equally delicate feel of the cover—just looking at my bed makes me want to crawl into it.”

The material (100% viscose from bamboo) has a breathable and smooth feel to it that’s nice for hot sleepers but also anyone who doesn’t want a more textured cover like linen. Even better, the soft, pastel-inspired color options like peony pink and laurel green make it a great fit for styling a bed during this blooming season. “The fabric is so delicate and dreamy that it reminds me of flower petals,” Alpert tells me. “Since I chose the peony colorway, it definitely fits the romantic profile.”

Even though it has a smooth texture, the comforter inside won’t slip around because of the secure snap closures. “Cozy Earth has 12(!) points of contact between the comforter and the cover, so there is no way anything is going to get loose, especially because these are snapped on, and not tied, like many other duvet covers,” she says. “I pair it with the bamboo viscose comforter with standard fill and the combination works great because the comforter has some weight and the duvet cover does not mess with it in any way.”

A darling of the 2010s direct to consumer movement, Parachute is a home brand best known for its bedding, though the company has also dabbled in furniture, mattresses, and other essentials. Its products, including the Linen Duvet Cover, are Oeko-Tex Standard 100–certified, meaning that every element (even buttons!) has been tested for substances damaging to human health. Parachute also doesn’t artificially soften their products. In the wrong hands, linen can be itchy or stiff until it’s been broken in, but that wasn’t the case here. This version, made of European Flax and made in the Guimarães region of Portugal, was inviting and oh so soft. The company also touts the material as naturally antimicrobial, which is a plus.

Another pick for a bohemian bedroom, this duvet cover has a lived-in look and several organic colors to choose from.

If you, in true minimalist fashion, like a monochrome bedscape, style this duvet cover with linen sheets in natural colors. If you want a slightly moodier bedroom, try a shade like cacao or indigo.

Contributor Lila Allen has nothing but good things to say about the feel of this linen and its nonchalant elegance: “I was pleasantly surprised at how soft this cover was—with linen, sometimes it can be a roll of the dice. This set had the best of both worlds: super supple but still casually elevated. The linen is a nice thickness, too; I can’t see any trace of the duvet inside of it.” Parachute’s linen has 175 GSM, and Quince’s linen that I mention down below has around 150 GSM. To Allen’s point, this means Parachute’s is more durable with a substantial feel and less opaque (the reason why she can’t see her duvet insert peeking through) with a lighter cover color like toast or sand.

Allen pairs her duvet cover with an all-season comforter from Riley, which she says stays secure through a button closure on the side and gives just the right amount of rumple together. The insert moves around a bit inside of the cover but mostly remains in place. “Best of all, I’ve been sleeping soundly with the set on hot nights as well as ones where the AC has been on overdrive, and so far it holds up in both situations—not too warm or cool.” Allen tells me that she shares a bed with her “hot-blooded husband and a large Maine Coon cat,” so her bed usually runs warm, so this layerable, snuggly cover is perfect.

The home brand is headquartered in New York City, however, the materials are sourced from fourth-generation, family-owned textile mills in Portugal and other countries across Europe. The products span a range of bedding and bath products, namely duvet covers, sheets, towels, mats, and other accessories like pillows and robs.

Since all of the duvet covers come in neutral, unfussy colors, this is a great option for minimalists.

I style this simply with other neutrals like white or cream sheets. When I want to add more visual interest, I layer in butter yellow bedding or a quilt in soft, muted tones.

To put it simply, this duvet cover feels like a lightweight cashmere sweater. It’s not stuffy, but it’s not flimsy either. Riley Home’s somehow managed to make a cover that feels airy enough for nights when my apartment’s radiator runs overly hot and still warm enough when I want to curl up in bed after a cold commute from work.

Even though it feels soft, it’s not made of pure cashmere. In reality, it’s made of 95% cotton and just 5% cashmere, but I wouldn’t have noticed if I didn’t read the label so closely. The texture has a brushed quality to it that feels gentle and light on my skin. There are a few neutral colors on the site. I went with the oatmeal and have liked styling it with white sheet sets so far for a simple, not-overly-done-up bedspread. A couple of other thoughtful details are the interior ties and buttons to keep my comforter from shifting inside. The super-easy care sold me too. The brand doesn’t recommend dry cleaning—just a machine wash and dry with a gentle detergent will do. As someone who has lugged specialty cashmere bedding to NYC cleaners on foot through the years, this note in and of itself almost convinced me to give the bedding a try.

Quince’s entire deal is about making high-quality luxury products at an affordable price. They work only with factories that are both sustainable and pay a fair wage, which is something that many shoppers care enough about to pay a little extra for, but Quince cuts back on things like fancy packaging to keep costs down.

Quince is another AD favorite for its plethora of prints and solid colors. Try this duvet cover in your space—no matter its design style—for a lightweight addition to your bedscape that’s also budget friendly.

Since linen makes a statement on its own with its lived-in look, I recommend styling this duvet cover with Quince’s classic European linen sheet set and a fluffy duvet insert in moody neutral hues (think deep brown) for a cozy sleep oasis. It’s also neutral enough that you can add some pattern sheeting for extra personality.

I’ve had this Quince linen duvet for about a year and it’s been a mainstay since it’s substantial and textured while still having an airiness to it—even when I’m layering with a few throw blankets or quilts when it’s cold outside. Sometimes linen gets a bad rap for its rough texture, but this best seller has been gentle against my skin and only gotten softer with more routine wear and care. It’s not as soft as something like an heirloom-quality stonewashed linen, but I’m not too picky in the linen department. I think its Oeko-Tex certification gives it a leg up generally to some competitors in this fabric category too.

I chose this Quince duvet since there were so many color options to choose from. I love moody colors year-round, and the burgundy is true to the deep color I saw on the site and it hasn’t faded after months of washes. It has the relaxed look you know and love with linen materials. Steaming it knocks out wrinkles easily whenever I want a more put-together look in my bedroom, though.

At this price point and with the most colors and prints available in this guide, I think this comforter cover can give you a great, budget-friendly way to dress a bed. The button closures also help keep a duvet insert or comforter in place. The care has been simple. I wash it with similar colors on a cold cycle and tumble dry on low and have only noticed a loose thread here and there, but nothing too crazy.

As mentioned above in our top overall pick, Brooklinen is known as the “home of the internet’s favorite sheets,” so we find it to be a worthy destination for quality bedding—including this quilt-like duvet cover made with 100% cotton.

With a design that mirrors the appearance of a quilt, we think this duvet cover would dress a vintage-inspired space beautifully—like the bedding you’d find in a historic Victorian home.

Alpert chose the plum colorway because of its sophisticated look that anchors her bedroom. She shares that the hue looks exceptionally well-paired with the deep caramel of the Boll & Branch Grand waffle blanket, as the color almost works like a moody neutral.

Even though the Brooklinen website describes this duvet as “breezy,” Alpert says it feels more like a weighted blanket. “The ribbed side is certainly quilt-like, which is not surprising because each ribbon that runs through the duvet cover is padded ever so slightly,” she shares.

The cover has a two-sided design: one side with textured, ribbed matelasse and the other with a crisp percale fabric. Alpert thinks this material combo is genius since it keeps the duvet cover from feeling too heavy. “This is especially key for anyone who sleeps without a flat sheet—you’ll feel like you’re getting into freshly changed linens night after night,” she says. “On the flip side, the ribbed texture elevates the duvet cover, not only in how it looks but it gives your bedding a slightly cushy sensation.”

Rest assured that the feel isn’t as heavy as an actual weighted blanket. Alpert says it certainly has substance and structure, though. “When I sleep with it on, it feels as if I am very secure—no one will dare wake me up,” she notes.

Hommey is a relatively new Australian-based brand that got its start in 2020. It became popular for robes and nightwear in bold, fashionable stripes. The designs are now spread across the bedding category, including cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers.

Since the brand is known for more out-of-the-box colorways across its collections, this duvet color is a great option for maximalists looking to experiment with bold color-blocking.

For a moodier bedscape, I style this duvet cover with sheets in a deep tone like burgundy. Overall, the chocolatey hue acts like a neutral and pairs beautifully with lighter sheet colors like oatmeal, which can also complement the cream-colored trim.

I know we’ve talked about linen a couple of times already in this story, but Hommey’s duvet helps hit the trifecta for the category. The natural flax fiber felt smoother and more broken-in than my Quince version right out the package. My guess is that it’s because of the stonewashed finish, which is known to give scratchy linen a more silky quality. I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes. The duvet caught my attention even more because of all of the styles. There are over 30 fashionable colors and prints, like the oxford and plum reversible cotton duvet I want in a button-down shirt version. The linen offering has four distinct colorways, including the brown sugar with cream trim that I got for myself. I like deep colors for my bedscape, especially as the year starts inching towards fall and winter, and its rich hue hasn’t disappointed. It's the perfect complement to my autumnal color palette, especially when I pair it with burgundy linen sheets.

It is less expensive than the Parachute pick and has a plusher texture than the Quince, so I’d say this is the perfect middle ground for an approachable but high-quality linen duvet.

Garnet Hill was founded in New Hampshire in the mid-1970s by Pegge and Grant Dowse who built the brand on a commitment to sustainable materials, thoughtful craftsmanship, and responsible sourcing with products like organic cotton and flannel bedding. The bedding blends traditional styles with a modern touch to fit in a range of bedrooms.

Our tester says the Pear Garden print is completely unexpected. “As much as I love florals, stripes, and gingham, a girl needs a break…and these charming pears are just the right motif,” Alpert shares. “They signal a cottagecore moment without going over the top. Every time I glimpse the cheery yellow fruit, I crack a little smile. Plus, the colorway of bold yellow, sage green, brown, and cream are easy to coordinate with the rest of my bedding collection.”

Because the pear motifs are the statement, we think you can go with more subtle sheets like a white set with embroidered trim. If you’re more of a maximalist, you can lean into the pattern play with a gingham sheet set in a complementary muted tone like brown and extra layers like a faux fur blanket if you’re cozying up for winter.

According to Alpert, this duvet cover is synonymous with cozy. It’s the softest option on this list because of the brushed flannel fabric, and it’s also a great pick if you live in cold climates since it has a bit of heft to it. “It’s as if a layer of leaves, or in this case pears, is surrounding me during winter hibernation,” she says. “That’s in part because this specific flannel is woven to have a substantial six-ounce weight.”

Alpert’s had this for nearly one year and says it has a decadent texture, likening it to climbing under a layer of meringue when she pairs it with her fluffy Ostermoor down duvet insert. “The plush feel of the cover also makes me think that I’ve just scored an upgrade to a royal suite,” Alpert adds.

At this point, she hasn’t noticed any pilling, but she does note that the cover is a bit snugger than a typical king, so you can expect the duvet to feel a little loftier than a regular fit.

What to Look for in the Best Duvet Covers

A duvet cover is more than just a bedcover. This eye-catching textile has a large footprint in any bedroom and can instantly give your space a refresh—whether with unique colors and prints or something more modest—especially if you want to disguise an old duvet insert. With this in mind, I tapped AD PRO Directory designers to weigh in on what to look for in a duvet cover to elevate your bedroom.

Material: When it comes to duvet covers, everyone has their own personal preferences. For Nicole R. Fisher, CEO and founder of Nicole Fisher Interiors, it’s linen: “They’re effortless, lightweight, and airy. I think the simplicity of the linen transcends different styles and spaces,” she says. Fisher notes that the feel is a big factor when selecting a duvet cover.

Carmen René Smith, founder and principal designer of Aquilo Interiors, says that it also needs to feel soft to the touch, breathable, and cozy. “What’s the point of a beautiful duvet if you don’t want to snuggle into it?” she says. “Texture is key too—whether it’s silky, crisp, or nubby, it should add depth to the space.”

Comfort: All of the interior designers I spoke to for this story point to natural fibers, not only because of their quality but also their airflow and breathability. Shelbie Cox of Shelbie Cox Studio recommends natural fibers like organic cotton and linen and notes that polyester and other synthetic fibers are best to avoid since they can trap heat.

Design: With so many patterns and colors to choose from, it’s important to keep your bedroom’s design style in mind. If you like more of a minimalist bedroom, Cox suggests a fine stripe pattern (like Quince’s European Linen Duvet Cover) or a monochromatic, muted color palette (see the Cozy Earth Bamboo Duvet Cover) for your duvet cover set.

If you want to go bold for your bedroom, there are options aplenty. “We’re maximalists, so we say bump up the color and pattern no matter what your signature style is!” says Smith, adding that it’s important to still maintain balance. “If you have bold wallpaper, pull a color from it and go for a solid, textured duvet—like a rich velvet for drama or a soft linen for a more relaxed vibe. If you’re mixing patterns, think about scale—a bold, oversized print pairs best with a smaller, more delicate duvet pattern to give the eye a place to rest.”

If you don’t want to commit to one style just yet, rest assured that having a few duvets in rotation can help you keep your bedroom design fresh. “I tend to go simple on bedding and let the accessories be the pops of pattern and color that’s easily swapped out,” adds Fisher.

Maintenance: While these are great design accessories for a bedroom, they also need to be practical. Ashley Ross, founder and principal designer of Muse Noire Interiors recommends keeping these questions in mind when shopping: How does it fasten (zipper, tie up, or buttons)? Does it fit within your washer and dryer? This will help you know how to use it and how to care for it.

We tested the best duvet covers the same way we test products for the rest of our sleep content: by bringing the items in our homes and dressing them on our beds. This way, you’re guaranteed to get a real-life look at how the products perform after weeks and months of everyday use. We also wash them routinely to keep an eye out for any wear and tear. All of the brands we feature reflect a variety of price points, designs, and materials so you have the best options to choose from for your bedroom.

Jump to the “How We Tested” section of this article to watch an in-depth video about our testing methodology and some of our favorite products and brands.

You don’t necessarily need a duvet cover. It depends on how you like to dress your bed. In my opinion, it’s a great bed accessory. A duvet cover not only protects your duvet insert but it also gives you the opportunity to easily switch up your bedscape (instead of swapping comforters when you want a new look). That said, pay attention to the care instructions for your insert because some do not recommend washing or dry cleaning.

There are several ways you can put a duvet cover on, but according to TikTok experts, this method below is as foolproof as possible:

Start by turning your duvet cover inside out, top side down, with the duvet opener at the foot of the bed. Then, place your comforter on top and secure the corners with the attached ties to the duvet cover. Starting at the head of the bed, roll the duvet down towards the foot just like a burrito. Finally, fold the duvet opening over each end of the roll, and unroll the blanket back towards the

Always check the manufacturer instructions to find out how to wash your specific duvet cover. However, the most common way to clean a duvet cover is by machine washing it with like colors with a gentle detergent on a cold cycle. If the duvet cover has a zipper closure, it's usually helpful to zip it closed to keep it from snagging in the washing machine.

It's generally recommended to wash your duvet cover as often as you wash your sheets, which is about once a week. If you use a top sheet, though, you can usually extend another week and wash your duvet cover every other week.

Our editors selected top products in this story from tried-and-true brands on the market, from Brooklinen to Boll & Branch. These brands boast organic materials like 100% organic cotton and European Flax and bamboo for a sustainably made bed. Plus, many boast eco-friendly certifications like GOTS and Oeko-Tex so you know they are free of chemicals. As a design editor, I also made sure all of the products have a range of colors, patterns, and prints to complement a bedroom’s style.
