#4857. Who Is the Best Surgeon?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

You have to undergo a major operation. You’re referred to a surgeon at a large medical center. How do you know if said surgeon is technically superior or even sufficiently proficient in their specialty? Who do you check with? Who would know for sure?

The scary answer is: No one may truly know. Very few people are in a position to judge the technical mastery of a given surgeon. For most specialties, there is no objective way to rate surgeon performance. Instead, we depend on the medical school/residency selection and education process and a couple of specialty board examinations to guarantee a certain level of competence in all surgeons—competence, not necessarily excellence. In fact, I would offer that the process results in a fair amount of variance in the judgment and technical prowess of its practitioners.

Against this backdrop, I have observed that the surgeons who are perceived as the most gifted in a given system are often simply those who tell everyone that they are “the best”—not necessarily the actual top performers. In other words, those perceived as the best are often those who aggressively impression manage (self-promote).

I have seen similar phenomena in non-surgical medical disciplines, in administrative hierarchies, academia, and the research world, and I suspect that it occurs in many other professions and organizations. Without meaningful objective supporting data and/or informed oversight, the quality of an individual’s work can be far from obvious, opening the door for external assessments to be influenced by more subjective factors—most commonly relentless self-promotion, but also PR efforts, internal politics, networking, nepotism, cronyism, favoritism, bigotry, prejudice, misogyny, etc. Thus, an individual’s reputation within a system and/or their profession may not reflect their actual proficiency, acumen, or prowess.

In competitive fields, this may negatively affect coworkers’ advancement and the achievement of their personal goals. For example, I have seen highly talented but self-effacing surgeons passed over for departmental advancement, academic promotion, national organizational positions, etc., in favor of their more vocal and self-aggrandizing but not necessarily technically superior colleagues.

For a high-achiever, witnessing an average or below-average performer soar past them in career success can be dispiriting, disincentivizing, and at times infuriating. Consider working in the shadow of a colleague who repeatedly seizes singular credit for joint effort, scoops up all internal and external recognition and kudos, and insists on allocation of resources to their own projects and interests.

For a surgeon, partnership with an aggressive self-promoter could potentially affect referral patterns, organizational support, academic status, ego, confidence, patient satisfaction (don’t most people want to be operated on by “the best”), and even liability. For an organization, advancement of such personnel could become stagnating and destabilizing, a source of rancor, frustration, burnout, diminished incentive, disrupted collaboration, and declining retention.

For these reasons, I have pushed my undergrads, medical students, and neurosurgical trainees to be aware of the impact of self-promotion on a career. One would hope that one’s good work will speak for itself and, indeed, quiet competence often does result in some recognition in various microenvironments, but the larger the setting, the higher the stakes, the more individual performance can get lost in the background noise, favoring those who draw attention to themselves. While I urge students and trainees not to feel that they have to compete with the most vocal, most self-aggrandizing of their colleagues, I advise them to inculcate a certain amount of self-promotion into their approach to their careers.

Against a backdrop of a hyper-busy, multitasking work environment, honest representation of one’s own capabilities and achievements is not only acceptable, but desirable. It will facilitate an individual’s realization of their career goals and help create a bulwark against job dissatisfaction and burnout. For an organization, it will give leadership a clear picture of the capabilities and strengths of its members. To this end, I advise you, as I do my students and trainees, to embrace a certain level of honest/transparent self-promotion.

It is OK to be proud of your skills and accomplishments. Make clear to multiple audiences your background, your training, your skills, your outcomes, your achievements—that is, what you are “bringing to the table.” At the same time, be willing to acknowledge your shortcomings, holes in your training, and arenas in which you would be better ceding control to, or asking for assistance from, your colleagues and other experts.

Avoid overt bragging or misrepresentation and the denigration of others—even sub-optimally performing self-promoters—but make sure your efforts and accomplishments are seen. It is OK, for example, to make such things clear to your chain of command. In fact, organizations are often anxious to feature the special talents and accomplishments of their members in their overall PR efforts.

Rather than walking around proclaiming your qualities, look for opportunities to simply put them on display. Perhaps you can volunteer to give talks and seminars, educating various groups (including the lay public), thus displaying your mastery of your field. Learn how to translate the complex and nuanced nature of your field for those not already in your lane of expertise.

Create a PR plan. Have an online presence—a website, a blog, educational videos, maybe even a podcast. Share your professional wisdom and thoughts. Be open to questions and discussion. Always be willing to teach but also to learn.

Broaden your skills through an openness to new or different approaches to the work environment you face and its challenges. Attend seminars and conferences. Connect and network there. Become known outside your micro-environment. Stay up on and even ahead of the curve in your areas of expertise. Find outlets to write about your efforts. Investigate opportunities to be interviewed in podcasts or on the radio or television.

If the light of recognition is shown on you, accept proudly the accolades, but spread them among those who support or work with you. In fact, feature, promote, and celebrate your team as much or more than yourself—it will reflect positively back on you.

#4856. What to Know About Intermittent Fasting and Your Workouts

Yes, you can use this approach and keep training—if you have the right strategy.

DIETING CAN BECOME complicated, fast. Eat this, don't eat that, only eat so much of this, and eat even less of that. When counting, tracking, and planning all start becoming too much, many turn to intermittent fasting as an alternative. It worked for Los Angeles Lakers superstar (and Men's Health digital cover star) Luka Dončić this summer, too, as it was a key part of the overall training and nutrition plan. Doncic, who has occasionally had his conditioning called into question during his NBA career, seems primed for a big season this fall for the Lakers.

While intermittent fasting may help simplify your meal-prep routine, you might find that the practice complicates your workout schedule. The premise of the intermittent fasting diet is simple: only eat for a small amount of time during the day, and fast the rest. There are several different kinds of intermittent fasting schedules, but the most popular one requires you to fast for 16 hours, then fit your meals into the next eight. Whatever food you eat during that period is up to you, so long as you stick within your eating window (though, filling up those few hours with several cheeseburgers and buckets of fries probably won’t get you very far in the weight loss department).

Food fuels our body for activity, though—and when you take that fuel away for most of the day, your workouts will likely suffer. You may find yourself feeling weak and lethargic in the gym when sticking to a fasting schedule, which is not ideal if you’re trying to build muscle mass and keep yourself in shape. That doesn’t mean you can’t work out when you’re fasting; it’s more a matter of proceeding safely in a way that will still optimize your training. A few small changes in your schedule and practices and you can continue your quest for that dream physique safely.

Let’s back up for a moment. First, it's important to understand the intermittent fasting schedule before you consider how to implement the strategy within a workout plan.

The most common type of intermittent fasting is the daily, time-restricting format. Typically, there’s a 16-hour fast, followed by an eight hour eating window. For example, someone could make their eating period between 12 p.m. and 8 p.m., only consuming lunch and dinner.

The time schedule can vary depending on your day. If you’re a person that needs more fuel in the morning, you may run on a 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. schedule instead. The time of day doesn’t really matter, as long as the consumption window sits at eight hours.

If that sounds like something you’re interested in trying, talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian first. Fasting is not appropriate for those that are pregnant, have a history of an eating disorder, or have certain medical conditions—speaking to your doctor will ensure the practice is a healthy choice for you.

If you frequently succumb to the temptation of a nighttime walk to the fridge, IF might just be the thing you need to keep your snacking in check and lose that excess weight.

“Intermittent fasting puts a cap on eating and can eliminate or minimize overconsumption at night. This can decrease calorie intake, can help with better sleep as the stomach won't be having a fiesta when it is time for a siesta,” says Leslie Bonci, R.D., M.P.H, sports dietician for the Kansas City Chiefs.

Weight loss isn’t the only benefit to the practice, though. There’s some evidence to suggest that intermittent fasting can reduce the risk of diabetes, lower blood pressure, and help maintain muscle mass.

That said, intermittent fasting is by no means the perfect diet for everyone, or a magic bullet for weight loss. For some, it’s a simple practice that may help eliminate those extra trips to the fridge. But for others, eating in a small window of time is just not sustainable— and the best diet is always one that keeps you consistent.

If fasting is that diet for you, exercise is vital to keep your heart healthy and muscles strong while dieting. Take these tips to schedule your workouts appropriately with your feeding hours.

Whether it’s a 5/2 protocol (eat for five days, fast for two) a 16/8 (fast for 16 hours, eat for eight), or any other version of IF, most people on a fasting diet wind up losing weight. That’s because it’s much harder to overeat if all your daily calories are crammed into an eight-hour window than if you can spread them out over 15 to 16 hours. That’s what makes IF such an effective weight-loss tool: by restricting the time frame in which you can eat, you effectively restrict the number of calories you take in as well.

But if your main goal is maximizing muscle, fasting isn’t a great idea. “Unless you’re a real novice, you can’t build appreciable muscle in a caloric deficit,” says Angelo Poli, ISSA, co-owner of Whole Body Fitness in Chico, CA, creator of the MetPro diet and exercise app. A pound here and there? Maybe. But you won’t build anywhere near as much as you would if you consume a few hundred extra calories above and beyond what your body needs each day. So don’t try. Your primary goal while fasting should losing fat. To build muscle, you need fuel.

Even if your main goal is losing fat, you still need to lift, which prevents your body from burning through muscle to fuel your daily activities. You won’t gain much muscle if you’re fasting, but if you lift, you won’t lose it, either. “The same activities that build muscle when you’re fueled help preserve it when you’re in a caloric deficit,” says Poli.

Since you’re only trying to maintain the muscle you have—not pack on additional beef—you can get away with a fairly infrequent lifting schedule—2 to 3 times per week, exercising your whole body each workout (try this routine).

Lifting weights, sprinting, doing CrossFit WODS, and other high-intensity activities all depend on carbohydrates for fuel, explains Poli. If you perform any of these activities during (or worse, at the end of) your fast, your performance will suffer. Instead of getting stronger and faster, you may well get weaker and slower.What to do? “If you’re a big guy with a lot of weight to lose, no big deal,” says Poli. “Go ahead and lift on an empty stomach. You might lose a little bit of muscle, but you’ll burn fat, too—and that’s your main goal.”If you’re a slimmer guy worried about your muscle definition, no need to worry— we have a solution for you too.

It’s vital that you eat before you workout so that you can get the most out of your lift, but depending on your build, it might be good to ensure a little something afterwards. “Eliminating the post-workout refueling may delay recovery as well as muscle protein and muscle glycogen resynthesis,” says Bonci. So, if you’re on the slimmer side and are worried about losing some of your muscle definition, it’s probably better to schedule your lifting workouts during your feeding window. So if you eat from noon to 8 p.m. each day, try to hit the gym around 5, then go home and eat a high-protein meal to ensure adequate recovery from your workout. Bonci suggests sandwiching your workout into your meals if you’re limiting calories. Meaning, eat one third of your meal before the gym, and the other two thirds of the meal afterwards. That way, you get some in before to power the workout, and the rest after to recover. “Ideally, food and fluid would parenthesize the workout,” she says. Overall, it’s best to do your best to fit your workout into your eating period so that you can have something before and after. If your schedule just doesn’t allow for it, it might be time to adjust the structure of your eating period— either by extending it, or changing the start and end times. “The window of eating may need to be longer to accommodate physical activity,” says Bonci.

While fasted lifting is a big fat mistake, fasted cardio is fine—but know that fat burning and fat loss are not the same. This means your body is burning fat as an energy source—and, without a calorie deficit, those stores will be replenished. Fasted cardio is safer than fasted weight training, though—since your body uses fat stores for slow, steady-state cardio activities. For best results, schedule those lifting sessions during or after your feeding windows, and schedule cardio before them.

The key to exercising safety while using IF is to listen to your body. If you’re starting to feel light-headed after hopping onto the treadmill for some fasted cardio, be smart about the situation and stop and grab some food and water until you feel okay to start again. Carry a snack in your gym bag, for example, just in case.

To ensure you’re following a program that fits best to your body, speak with your doctor before starting up any new diet or workout program. They will be able to help you determine what will be safe and effective for you.

He lives in Los Angeles with his wife and their two children.

#4855. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

#4853. The Importance of Giving Thanks

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

I wrote a book on 365 days of self-care to offer empaths and highly sensitive people simple exercises to boost their energy, open their hearts, and stay centered. Self-care is essential for all sensitive people. When you practice it mindfully and lovingly every day, your sensitivities will flourish. The self-care practices I present as daily offerings in Thriving as an Empath will support you in being a compassionate empath without trying to “fix others.” Below is an excerpt from the book on the importance of gratitude.

This is a beautiful time of year to be grateful for your blessings. Gratitude is a spiritual act. You are sending a message to loved ones, colleagues, the natural world, and spirit that you are thankful for them. It opens the heart for you to experience more love.

Even if you perceive your life as lacking, just for today, humbly focus on your blessings. Ask yourself, “What am I grateful for? My health? Physical mobility? Clarity of mind? Or the capacity to love, despite all the challenges I’ve faced?” What about your friends, family, and animal companions? Or your home, car, job, and healthy food?

Then inwardly declare, “I am grateful for my life. I am grateful for everyone who loves me, and whom I love. I am grateful for the earth, the birds, the sky, and the oceans.” Feel free to add to this list in any way that applies to you. In addition, you can express your gratitude directly to others by saying, “Thank you for being in my life. You have enhanced it more than you can know.” A simple expression of appreciation means so much.

Also have gratitude and love for yourself: The way you move, the way you eat, the way you look, the way you relate to others. It’s too easy to slip into self-criticism or focus on a glass being half-empty. Recognize that temptation and choose to reject it in favor of acknowledging blessings. Life is so amazing and beautiful. Seeing yourself and others through the eyes of love and gratitude generates a sense of contentment with yourself and others.

Today—and really, every day—is a sacred opportunity for thanksgiving.

I will focus on all I have to be grateful for,And allow my heart to feel content and full.I will be thankful for the love in my life.

#4851. Learning Emotion Regulation... From a Horse?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Strong human emotions are often difficult to manage, and learning to control them is never easy. Most skeptics would assume that no animal, let alone a horse, could help us humans develop emotion regulation… but they can.

Unlike humans, with our over-reliance on vision, horses navigate the world primarily through smell and touch. The average horse has all the neurological machinery to detect and interpret odors that a bloodhound has. Bloodhounds, just for reference, can detect an odor that’s 12 days old from 12 miles away. Not bad, given that we humans can barely sniff out raw steak on the kitchen counter.

The average horse also has exquisite touch sensitivity. Many areas of her skin can detect a lighter touch than the human fingertip is capable of feeling. She can sense a rider turn his head a couple inches to the left or right, even when he’s invisible up in the saddle. She notices the slightest touch of a single finger on her reins and the barest pressure of the rider’s legs against her sides. The weights and pressures horses can detect often exceed human capacity.

OK, so horses are cool. But what do these sharpened senses have to do with emotional regulation? Everything. Horses are emotional mirrors. They pick up human emotions instantly using smell and touch, then reflect them to the human rider or handler through equine body language. Remember, horses are herd animals, accustomed to reading the slightest nuances from their companions.

Let’s suppose you’re travelling along one day on a horse you ride often. Gator notices through feel that your muscles are more tense than usual, your joints feel stiff, and you aren’t quite as forgiving with your hands. His prey brain tells him maybe something is wrong. Now, a prey animal like a horse can’t afford to ponder your tension; to survive a potential predatory chase, he has to run now. Maybe you have sensed some danger that he doesn’t know about yet, and using good herd behavior, Gator doesn’t want to wait around and find out.

So… he becomes tense, stiff, and less forgiving. His head shoots up, his ears prick forward, his mouth hardens, and his nostrils open wide to sniff the air for danger. His muscles turn from butter to concrete. He is mirroring your nervousness with anxiety of his own, and sitting astride a 1,200-pound animal that’s seven or eight feet long, you will feel his anxiety immediately.

As a rider, you can’t afford to allow Gator to maintain that high level of anxiety. Soon, he will explode in fear—bolting, spinning, bucking—and you will hit the dirt, likely breaking a few bones in the process. That’s why horses and riders have to notice each other’s emotions.

It also explains why we have to regulate our human emotions when working with horses, whose brains are driven primarily by fear even under the best circumstances. To accommodate that physiology, the rider or handler must remain relaxed. So, much of learning to ride a horse is learning to manage our human emotions. When we aren’t sure what we feel (nervous? scared? weak? fluttery?), our horses tell us.

Sometimes while riding, I notice that a horse is nervous and wonder why. It could be his temperament, background, former training, feed, the weather, deer in the distance, or any number of things. But often it’s because I’m nervous about something and don’t know it. Perhaps business responsibilities concern me, maybe a frenemy just drove in, or sometimes I’m in a hurry to make my next appointment or make a call to offset the latest family drama. Any of these situations can cause nervous human tension, anger, or frustration, all of which the horse can feel.

Horses tell us with their bodies that our human tension exists, and they show us how it feels. To calm a horse, we have no choice but to calm ourselves. We breathe deeply and loud enough that the horse hears us (for he will also mirror our breath), we train our muscles to relax even when we’re worried, we lower our shoulders and soften our necks, and we allow our bodies to move more fluidly to match the horse’s normal movement.

Do that every day with a huge, powerful animal, and… yep, you will learn to regulate your emotions. From a horse!

#4849. The 11 Best Golf Bags Our Gear Editors Have Tested

It's time to retire your ancient, beat-up golf bag once and for all.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHILE YOU MAY not think about it, in many ways a golf bag can make or break your golf game. Sure it doesn't have any real performance value like a set of golf clubs or golf shoes do, but what makes a golf bag so important is its ability to help you carry your gear from point A to point B, with as little energy exerted as possible. And, if you’ve ever walked a full round of 18 with a crummy bag, then you’ll know exactly how it can take a toll on your game.

But, the best golf bag is going to be one you hardly notice. Confusing? Think about how a bad golf bag can impact your play. Maybe the shoulder strap always digs into your neck when carrying. Or perhaps your bag is too thin and flimsy, so you have to wrangle the heck out of it so it will stay put on the back of the cart. Poorly made kickstand or clubs don't go in and out smoothly? Not enough storage capacity to carry all your gear like rangefinders, your phone, and everything in between. That’s just the tip of the iceberg.

From an aesthetic perspective, you’ll want to opt for a golf bag that fits your stylistic choice, and on today’s market, there’s an option for every personality. Plus, thanks to the boom of golf in the last few years, finding a golf bag with style points is not a problem, especially as more and more brands emerge with an emphasis on visuals and aesthetics. We're seeing some truly standout designs from brands we absolutely love. Ahead, we've pulled together our latest guide to the best golf bags based on years of testing we've been doing on the course and at the range.

You really can't go wrong with a Callaway golf bag, but when it comes to which one provides the biggest bang for its buck, it's the flagship Fairway C. The newly designed model includes boosted storage all around, from the clubs (it can hold at least 14) to the pockets (7 spacious zippered compartments). What's amazing is the Fairway C still maintains a slim silhouette and a lightweight design (just four pounds in weight total). The bag is also waterproofed to the nines thanks to its water-resistant material and seam-sealed zippers.

A few more elite features we like include: Boosted protection for clubs thanks to soft rubber dividers and hard Shaft Shield rubber, a flexible base made to better sit on different surfaces and slopes, and a comfortable dual strap system for carrying.

If you are looking for a bag that pushes the envelope on style and innovation, then this is a solid choice.

The Ping Hoofer has been one of the best stand bags for years because it's simply solid at what it does. The comfortable double strap carrying system is intuitive and simple to use, the leg mechanisms are smooth and have never caused me issues, and there are plenty of pockets and storage for both walking and riding.

I've logged lots of miles walking with this bag over my shoulders, and one standout is the water bottle holder—it's positioned in a perfect location for me to reach slightly down with my left hand to grab and swig while I'm walking. The stow-away rain hood is also extremely handy and has saved some wet rounds over the years. While neither of these features are exclusive to the Hoofer, they're done in smart and high-quality ways that make this bag a standout.

While it's not the lightest stand bag in our guide at 5.5 pounds, it's still only 5.5 pounds and I've never felt it's too heavy. And the versatility it provides by being a great cart bag is too important to ignore. I have quite a few friends who still have their Ping Hoofers made in the early 2000s, and while they have some wear and tear on them, these bags are made for the long haul.

Read More: Garmin Approach S70 Golf Watch Review

Sunday Golf has quickly risen as one of the top bag makers in the game. At the center of its lineup is the Loma Bag, an ultra-lightweight bag (under 2 lbs) that's perfect for carrying the essentials on a par 3 or for taking to the driving range. The Loma Bag is great for the golfer who is looking for a side bag for those previously stated uses, but to really have enough space to play a round with, we love the Loma XL.

Like the Loma Bag, the Loma XL is built to stay lightweight. The XL is heavier than the Loma Bag (3.4 pounds to 2 pounds), but still lighter than pretty much all other golf bags in this guide. The XL comes with a double strap for comfortable walking on the course, a three-way top divider for keeping up to eight clubs organized, and an insulated frosty pocket for keeping your cold ones, well, cold.

It's minimalist, making it great for beginners and for those who don't want to deal with clutter or deal with carrying too much weight. The downsides are, of course, the ability to only carry up to eight clubs. If you pack the bag too full, you also risk putting too much weight on the pop-out stands.

The price point of under $200 really sells the Loma XL as a value-driven pick. It's not a Big Bertha bag, but it will carry what you need for the course—all while making sure you stay lean and mean. Start here if you want a trimmed-down golf bag, or if you are a beginner to the game and are still working from a small rotation of clubs.

The Titleist Players bags are a golfer favorite through each iteration. The Players 5 Stand is a sturdy stand bag with a low profile, promising plenty of storage without getting too ridiculous in size and organization. You get plenty of storage space (full-length drink pockets and apparel pockets), Velcro spots for easy glove storage, and an overall weight of 4.3 pounds. And just like the iconic hat, you get the classic cursive styling on the side of the bag.

The new feature on the Players 5 (that wasn't on the Players 4 bag) is a five-way top cuff. The extra compartment for club organization allows the ability to carry a few more clubs, so bring on the extra wedges and woods.

Really the only downside to consider is the cost. The Players 5 is about $40 more than the Callaway Fairway C—a similar golf bag in terms of configuration. If you're willing to pay up just a little more, then you can do no wrong going with this timeless pick.

Vessel Golf has long made some of the best golf bags out there. For years the brand would make bags for Tour pros that just didn't receive labels (so under the radar). In the past few years, though, the Southern California company branched out to the direct-to-consumer market and the response has been overwhelmingly good.

The Lux Stand is a new 2025 model that redefines what a stand bag can be: a rotator stand system that creates an extremely stable base, an internal base divider that reduces club jams even when the legs are out, a matching cart strap sleeve for when you ride, an umbrella holder, and so much more.

We've had a tester trying this one out this summer and it has wowed in every aspect. The details are also premium at a price that's about $100 more than some of the other stand bags in our guide. But everything feels extremely bespoke and premium.

TaylorMade makes several types of golf bags for those who want a deluxe carrier, but really the brand shines the most with its Golf Pro Cart Bag. Its sub-$230 price tag makes it super affordable for a quality cart bag that has everything one would want: comfortable shoulder straps, ample club storage, and generous pocket space.

Its nylon material and streamlined pocket space makes it easy to move and carry. The bag also has a 14-way top. The downside is this bag is not very waterproof. There are no innovative features or special details on this bag that make it standout. Instead, this is a classic cart bag that will get the job done and look good on the course—all for a generous price point.

Amazon has a lot of wallet-friendly golf bags, but if you are going to go the affordable route it's best to avoid the cheapest of the cheap. This bag from GoHimal is just a tad more expensive than the other Amazon brands, yet it still promises a sub-$150 price.

It's built with a 14-way top, so you can stuff an entire set of clubs inside (although remember it's one club per slot so it can be limiting/frustrating). You get a double strap for better carrying and decent pocket space (it even comes with a cooler pocket). Most reviews deem the kickstand to be sturdy, which is significant due to the amount of cheap golf bags out there that have weak and wobbly stand legs. What's nice is even the bottom of the bag is strong and capable of staying upright in a golf cart.

One negative to consider is the polyester material of the bag. It's durable and tear-resistant, but it isn't super rain resistant. So the bag is prone to getting soaked. Second is the logo; though the "Himal" reading on the side isn't ugly (a lot of the cheap Amazon golf bags have tacky logos and designs), it still is super large and visible.

If you are a golfer on a budget, then this bag warrants a look. If you are rocking expensive clubs, look for a golf bag that has more protective reinforcement features and better rain resistance. That's the verdict.

Ghost Golf first caught our attention via its cool magnetic golf towel. It turns out Ghost makes a mean golf bag, too.

The Anyday Katana is a one-of-a-kind storage monster with tons of pocket space and a 14-club carrying capacity. Subtle features like velvet-wrapped top dividers and cooler-lined water bottle sleeves (on both sides) make days on the course that much more fun. The bag is outfitted with carbon fiber legs so it can stand with authority, and it comes in a waterproof material that has a beautiful leather-like texture.

If you want luxury and premium storage, this is your bag right here.

Stitch Golf improved upon its original SL2 bag by giving it nearly 50 percent more storage while still staying under 5 pounds. The expanded storage means smoother pulls and inserts of clubs from the bag, which goes a long way when you find yourself repeating that motion a zillion times throughout a full round of golf.

We also like the designated pocket space. There's a larger compartment for apparel (like rain gear), a magnetized ball pocket that can store up to 12 golf balls, and a felt-lined pocket to store your phone and valuables.

The coolest detail about Stitch Golf's bags? It's super easy and low cost to add personalization features. For $10 more, you can add an initial patch that reads either horizontal or vertical.

Malbon has a fantastic take on its golf style, sitting at the intersection of country club and streetwear that’s neither vintage golf nor luxury resort (it also doesn’t hurt to have Jason Day representing the brand on Tour, either). Yet, it can portray all of those vibes somehow, very well might I point out, and its forest green cart bag does just that. This bag looks like it would be right at home at Augusta National Golf Club just as it would at your local course. This bag is more than just a looker, as its textured PU leather build looks lux, yet is weather-resistant enough to handle rainy conditions—and a hood cover, too. Though its listed as a cart bag, it has removable padded shoulder straps if you decide to walk a round and plenty of zippered pockets to hold all of your gear.

When traveling with golf clubs, you absolutely have to make sure your clubs are protected. I've been testing out Vessel's latest Travel Case 2.0 and it hasn't disappointed. While hard cases will almost certainly provide near-guaranteed protection, they're not totally necessary and are more expensive.

What's great about this soft case from Vessel is that it breaks down to a tiny square the size of its base for super easy storing. When you're limited on space in the garage or even just in the hotel room during your travels, not having to figure out where the heck to store a giant plastic case on wheels is a situation you'll be glad to avoid.

There is a fully padded top, reinforced runner guards on the back, rugged wheels that glide easily, and compression straps to really help keep everything in place. Keep in mind you will need to pick up a travel club protector separately, but once you do you can travel anywhere on any flight with peace of mind that your clubs are well-protected.

Golf bags essentially fall into two categories: cart bags and stand bags.

A cart bag is meant for cart use, which means they're designed for carrying on the back of a golf cart or on a hand (or roller) cart when walking the course. Cart bags are usually larger and contain more organizational space. The downside is they're heavier and, hence the name, you need to rent a cart (or prepare for some serious energy exertion when carrying around a course, which we don't recommend).

A stand bag is meant for carrying on your back. They typically have better strap designs (double straps) and are more lightweight. They also have a kickstand for keeping the bag upright when setting the bag down to pull out your clubs. The downside to a stand bag is less club space (the bag has to accommodate a kickstand placement) and less pocket space. It should also be noted that stand bags can be used when riding in a cart or using a hand cart. These are the most common bags amateur golfers use and are our recommended choice for the versatility they offer.

The number of dividers on your golf bag depends on how many clubs you like to play with. If you play with a full set of 14 clubs (which is what most golfers typically do), a 14-way divider is not necessarily the way to go—this requires a more precise in-and-out grabbing of clubs as each divider can only house one club. This means you can't just toss a club in the bag and keep moving, which can slow things down and even frustrate at times.

The most common divider types are four- and five-way. A common theory to organizing your clubs easily utilizes this layout: woods in the big compartment, long and mid irons together, short irons and wedges together, and the flat stick (aka putter) in a slot on its own. While this is by no means a rule, grouping like clubs together is a simple way to make use of your bag's space.

It's worth mentioning waterproofing because this characteristic can raise or lower the overall price of a golf bag. If you're golfing a lot or have an expensive set of clubs, then it's probably worth investing in a waterproof bag (and certainly one with a rain hood). Some waterproof bags are better than others, with seam-taped zippers and waterproof pockets. Other bags usually just have water-resistant shells.

If you aren't golfing a lot or if you have a more inexpensive club set, then waterproof features might not be that important. You can save some money by opting for a golf bag that's not fully waterproof, then if you're caught in the rain while playing you can simply put a plastic poncho over your clubs or buy some sort of rain hood to help protect the clubs.

While I may not be the most avid golfer on our MH staff, the one thing I do ensure I am consistent with is staying up on golf trends and style, which also means knowing the latest gear and brands. This serves as an excellent baseline for my research to ensure each pick not only looks fantastic on the course, but will perform to the standards you need them to.

I also partnered with our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower, who is an avid golfer, and a not-too-shabby mid-handicapper. Along with a few other golfers at Men's Health, we tested golf bags while walking 18, on 72-hole golf trips across the country, riding in carts, and playing pitch and putts.

We started with the golf bags we've been using and testing throughout the years, and then researched and got our hands on some new models as well as ones that we have yet to try out. We evaluated well over a dozen golf bags for this year's iteration of this guide based on comfort, durability, performance, and price point. Then we narrowed it down to the 11 best golf bags to satisfy any golfer's demands.

#4848. Michael Strahan Shares the Words That Helped His Daughter Through Brain Cancer Treatment

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Michael Strahan appeared in commercials for St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital, delivering a message he never imagined would become so personal: “No parent should have to hear that their child has cancer.”

But in 2023, the beloved TV host and former NFL player faced that reality when his daughter, Isabella, was diagnosed with brain cancer at 19 years old.

“[That] line that I used to deliver, usually at the end of the commercial…here I am actually filling that line in my life in real time,” Strahan told Healthline.

Strahan believes his longtime connection with St. Jude was more than a coincidence. After years of advocating for families affected by childhood cancer, he found himself on the other side of that experience.

“When I needed that family…they were there for me,” he said. “I’m just appreciative, and I think things come back to you; give out good, good comes back.”

In October 2023, Isabella began experiencing vomiting, headaches, and balance issues during her freshman year at the University of Southern California (USC). Tests revealed that she had medulloblastoma, a fast-growing cancerous brain tumor located in the cerebellum. She underwent emergency brain surgery, radiation therapy, and four rounds of chemotherapy.

While medulloblastoma typically occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 9, it can also affect young adults like Isabella.

“[The] biology in adolescents and young adults can differ meaningfully from pediatric cases, requiring specialized expertise at centers of excellence for this disease,” Arnab Chakravarti, MD, director of the Brain Tumor Program at The Ohio State University, told Healthline.

Medulloblastoma is sometimes confused with glioblastoma, the most common type of malignant primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma is particularly aggressive, with a median overall survival of just 15 months and a 5-year survival rate of less than 10%.

However, Chakravarti explained that medulloblastoma has a significantly higher cure rate than glioblastoma.

“[This is] a point of genuine hope that deserves to be communicated clearly,” he said.

Radiation therapy is a cornerstone of medulloblastoma treatment. Isabella received proton therapy, which uses precisely targeted radiation to treat tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue.

“For medulloblastoma, this physical precision is transformative,” Chakravarti said. “Proton craniospinal irradiation dramatically reduces [collateral] exposure — preserving cochlear function and hearing, reducing cardiovascular risk, protecting the thyroid, and most critically, sparing developing brain tissue in ways that translate into measurably better neurocognitive outcomes years after treatment.”

He added that multiple prospective studies have shown that children and young adults treated with proton craniospinal irradiation experience less cognitive decline and better quality of life compared to those treated with conventional radiation.

Today, Isabella is back at USC, embracing the everyday routines she once had to put on hold.

“I am back at USC, so…it’s been great, in the midst of exams, so it’s a little stressful, but I actually [am] inviting the stress in because at one point I didn’t have exams, so I’m happy to be back,” Isabella told Healthline.

Along with attending classes, Isabella is enjoying activities such as working out and cooking. She continues to undergo MRI scans of her head and spine every three months, but said that after another year, the scans will become less frequent, occurring every six months.

“But really…I don’t have a lot of doctor’s appointments,” she said.

“It feels like a brand-new life, but it’s a good one. And that’s wonderful,” Isabella said.

Isabella said her family’s support played an important role in helping her through cancer treatment. Spending so much time together in the hospital brought them closer as they watched movies and played cards and board games to pass the time.

“[It] really, really bonds you to people, and just having my dad and my whole family there was something that [you] can’t beat,” she told Healthline.

Michael said that despite the difficult circumstances, he cherishes the time he spent with his daughter. Before her diagnosis, Isabella was a typical teenager who spent much of her time at school or with friends.

“They say you spend the most time with your kid for the first few years of their life, and then once school starts, you don’t get a chance to spend as much time as you would like with them,” he said.

While Michael said he and Isabella already had a close relationship, her diagnosis brought the family even closer and helped them reflect on what mattered most.

“[What] was really important was family, and relationships, and the love that you have for each other, and the support you have to give each other,” he said. “I think that our relationship now is better than ever.”

Today, Michael makes an effort to visit Isabella at USC whenever he’s in Los Angeles during the NFL season.

“Some weekends she [has time for me]. Some she doesn’t,” he said. “But just to have that relationship with your child, where they want to hang out with you, is a good feeling, and that’s the relationship that we have.”

Michael and Isabella are sharing their story to raise awareness about brain cancer and offer hope to other families facing similar challenges.

They recently participated in a fireside chat in New York City hosted by Real Chemistry and SMAC, where they discussed their family’s experience navigating Isabella’s diagnosis, mental health, caregiving, and the impact of sharing their story.

Throughout her treatment, Isabella also documented her experience through a series of YouTube vlogs and the ABC primetime documentary, “Life Interrupted: Isabella Strahan’s Fight to Beat Cancer.”

For Michael, helping others is a value he learned from his parents. He recalled how his father used his transportation business in Germany to support people in need after retiring from the military.

“[He] would take donations, and use his money and his trucks, and drive stuff to Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, and drop it off there at local churches and the shelters for people, who he had no connection with,” said Michael. “So for me, I think I do what I feel is on my heart and what’s important to me.”

For parents caring for children with cancer, Michael emphasized that it’s OK to feel overwhelmed or emotional. He encouraged them to show their children love and support while helping them maintain hope for the future.

“I think positivity is the main thing because it was so tough on her at the time when she was [saying], ‘I can’t do it. I can’t do this. I can’t do that,’” said Michael.

Michael said he made a conscious effort to replace words like “can’t” and “if” with “when” while encouraging Isabella during treatment.

“Anytime she got down on herself, I’d say, ‘when you go back to college, when you do this, when you do that,’” said Michael. “And I just think the positive attitude and the love that you can give and the confidence that you can display towards your loved one [or] your child who’s going through something like this is the only thing you can do because you’re at the mercy of medicine.”

Now in her senior year at USC, Isabella is looking ahead to life after graduation.

“[There’s] a lot of interesting opportunities and things that I want to pursue,” she said.

Michael has no doubt she will find her way.

“She’s so talented, and this experience, in my opinion, has opened up my eyes to more talent that she has that I didn’t realize…the talent to connect people, and be in front of a crowd. I always thought she’d be nervous because I get nervous, but she’s better than me,” he said.

#4847. Inside the Facilities Powering the NWSL’s Next Generation

Teams are making investments in their athletes.

The National Women’s Soccer League has proven to be a force in women's sports. And around the league, exciting new performance facilities are popping up that are built specifically for its athletes. After all, think about how much of a player’s work week happens here, from lifting before practice to treatment afterward.

These facilities are designed with women in mind, from training and recovery needs to thoughtful inclusions for moms and caregivers (looking at you, Kaiser Permanente Performance Center). For players juggling practice and treatment with the demands of growing and raising a family, those details can make the job a little easier.

Some are brand new, and others are still being built. Here’s a look at the facilities powering the NWSL's evolution.

The Portland Thorns' new facility is shared with a WNBA expansion team, the Portland Fire. Women’s Health recently toured the new space and took careful note of all of the female-centric details.

It features tall ceilings, a spa-like color palette, and large windows that let in plenty of natural light. There's also a 17,000-square-foot gym with two full-size outdoor soccer pitches, a yoga and pilates studio, and custom Portland weight racks, along with resort-like contrast therapy tubs and locker rooms boasting extra-wide cabinets. The nursing room is outfitted with the rocking chair that Thorns star Sophia Wilson has in her daughter's nursery, and strollers and high chairs are available to use.

While Angel City FC shares BMO Stadium with Los Angeles FC, the team acquired a dedicated performance center located on the campus of California Lutheran University in 2024. Sitting on nine acres with approximately 50,000 square feet of indoor space, it’s the largest performance facility in the NWSL.

This space, which once hosted the Los Angeles Rams, underwent a multi-million dollar custom remodel to the interior and outdoor spaces to customize it for Angel City’s needs. Amenities include a massive gym stocked with the latest in performance tech, a dedicated hydrotherapy area, a children’s playroom, a content studio, and an outdoor relaxation lounge.

Like Angel City, Bay FC shares its stadium. But the team is opening a new 8.5-acre performance and training center on Treasure Island in San Francisco. It's slated to open in early 2027.

Early photos released by Bay FC show a stunning facility with lots of natural light, a 360-degree view of San Francisco, and a distinct spa-like vibe. In addition to performance and recovery resources, there will also be space dedicated to career development, education, and business training.

Home to the Kansas City Current, this stadium is the world's first privately-financed stadium dedicated solely to a professional women's sports team. CPKC Stadium has 11 local food and drink partners, giving fans a taste of Kansas City at games. The stadium was designed to have no seat further than 100 feet from the pitch, too. Among other unique features is that the home locker room is built with an oval layout to make every player feel like an equal part of the team.

“Every player who comes and plays in that stadium, every little kid, will have a completely different expectation now of what it means to be a professional female athlete,” team founder Angie Long told WH in 2024. “Once something like this is built…you can’t unsee it.”

Next summer, the defending NWSL champions will move into the former Red Bull New York training facility in Whippany, New Jersey. The yet-to-be-renamed space will be the club’s first dedicated training facility.

Expected amenities include three grass playing surfaces (one heated, with plans for an indoor turf field to come), a 3,000-square-foot gym, a player recovery room, and a dining area with meals prepared by a performance chef.

#4846. Why Trying to Control People Often Backfires

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

The holidays have a way of resurfacing family conflict. Whether we’re arguing about politics, religion, or putting pineapple on pizza, telling someone what to think rarely changes their mind. In fact, it typically makes them fight back harder. I’ve witnessed this reaction as a father, physician, White House adviser, and public health advocate—especially when disease outbreaks erode public trust.

During the pandemic, public health mandates seemed to intensify suspicions among people who were already skeptical of the government and vaccines. Americans adopted an "us-versus-them" mentality and stopped listening to anyone with an opposing view.

Scientists have a name for this: psychological reactance—the tendency to push back against restrictions that interfere with our freedom. Even when rules are meant to keep us safe, we resist because we don’t want someone else making decisions for us.

The sense that our autonomy is under threat dampens activity in the brain’s prefrontal cortex, which is involved in reasoning and synthesizing new information. This reduces our openness to evidence and explains why relying solely on control tends to backfire.

Curiosity, on the other hand, engages the brain's learning and reward systems. When we are invited to explore the benefits and risks of a decision, rather than being told what to think, the brain’s prefrontal cortex activity is enhanced and we become more open to considering new information. Our brains become primed to learn, making uptake of behavior more likely.

Put another way, while pressure engages threat circuits, curiosity engages learning circuits in our brains. That’s important because while control may push people to comply, it doesn’t establish the trust required to build lasting change.

During the pandemic, my Rishi Uncle was furious about government restrictions that had forced his motel business to shut down. He distrusted the government and listened to political commentators whose views were very different from mine.

As a physician working to protect people against COVID, I found his position deeply frustrating. I wanted him to understand the science and recognize the danger the virus posed to him and his family.

But I was so frightened that I didn't have the conversation I needed to have with him. My father did.

Rather than trying to change Rishi Uncle's beliefs, my father approached him with curiosity. As I listened to them speak, I started learning more about my uncle’s perspective. He watched as loved ones fell ill and died, feeling helpless. As a business owner, his livelihood was also under serious threat.

Despite his anger toward the government, my uncle wore a mask when he left the house and eventually got vaccinated. He recognized the risks facing himself and his family and made choices to protect them. He didn't have to change all his political beliefs to change his behavior.

Looking back, I wish I'd spent less time feeling frustrated with my uncle and more time trying to understand him. People may disagree about politics or personal freedoms, but they can often find common ground in protecting the ones they love.

Every tough conversation doesn’t end with a resolution, but it also doesn’t have to end with a blowout fight. While working with patients and communities, I’ve developed a few approaches to navigate disagreement in a healthier and more productive way.

Resist the urge to immediately correct someone when they say something you disagree with. Instead, ask them to identify their biggest concern: "What worries you most about this?"

Understanding the story behind someone’s beliefs and fears provides the context you need to address their concerns without alienating them in the process.

In the same vein, explaining how your own experiences have shaped your opinion can help someone see your point of view. Personal stories help people feel seen and heard and create opportunities to find common ground, shared experiences, and values, even if your opinions conflict.

Remember, you don’t have to change someone’s beliefs to change their behaviors. Someone who distrusts the government may still choose to get vaccinated to protect their family. A driver who thinks the speed limit is too low may still slow down to keep neighborhood children safe.

Try identifying the values you share—like protecting your family and friends—instead of demanding they agree with every issue.

In late 2023, I spoke at a symposium organized by Boston University and Harvard Medical School about lessons learned during the COVID pandemic. My panel focused on how to communicate important health information and counter misinformation.

That’s when I had a thought: Are we spending too much time trying to figure out why people are not listening to public health experts and not enough time listening to what they have to say?

This is one of the most important questions we can ask ourselves when we’re in a disagreement. It helps us shift from control to curiosity, accepting we may be wrong, listening to someone else’s perspective, and being open to a conversation that doesn’t end with a "winner."

Trust grows only when we’re willing to listen to each other. So, next time you’re frustrated that someone isn’t listening to you, consider how much you’ve done to try to understand them.

Steindl, C., Jonas, E., Sittenthaler, S., Traut-Mattausch, E., & Greenberg, J. (2015). Understanding psychological reactance: New developments and findings. Zeitschrift für Psychologie, 223(4), 205–214. https://doi.org/10.1027/2151-2604/a000222

Panjabi, R. (2026). Safer: A playbook—turning fear into action and crisis into community. HarperOne.

#4845. Artists Helen Marden and the Late Brice Marden Refashioned a Decommissioned 19th-Century Ferry Terminal

Over the course of their more than 50-year marriage, artist Helen Marden and her late husband, the eminent painter Brice Marden, amassed an international collection of seriously eccentric—and deeply magical—houses, gardens, and studios, each designed around the double helix of art and family. They bought their first house, a cliffside cottage on the Greek island of Hydra, in 1973, and since then real estate and art have been entwined in their life, art facilitating the purchase of property, the properties both catalyst and carapace for the evolution of their art. An Italianate villa in upstate New York, a pair of traditional riads in Marrakech, a hotel set among the ruins of a 19th-century sugar plantation in the Caribbean, a second house by the port in Hydra, a Renaissance Revival town house in Manhattan, a stately manse on a sprawling estate in Pennsylvania—every one of their idiosyncratic properties has its own fascinating history, reflected in its interior. The homes are all documented in the upcoming book Brice & Helen Marden: Houses, Gardens, Studios (Gagosian), edited by this writer, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson.

Helen Marden in the living room. Chair and side table by the Campana Brothers. The chimney is clad in Clé Tile. A watercolor by Henri Michaux rests on the mantel.

The living room includes chairs by Marcel Wanders (far left) and the Campana Brothers. Sculpture at right by Matthew Wang.

In the dining room, a Paavo Tynell pendant hangs above a rustic farm table with chairs by Jonathan Olivares and Maarten Baas. Amazonia marble covers one wall.

The Mardens were instinctively drawn to residences with endurance, places that have seen a few things, not newly built pleasure domes devoid of texture and soul. Swan House, the riparian hideaway in the middle of the Hudson River, epitomizes the couple’s embrace of the strange and the enchanted. Accessed by a long, narrow causeway that leads off the shore of Saugerties, the structure was built in 1877 as part of Long Dock, a ship terminal and moorage for large vessels conveying people and goods the length of the Hudson. It was also a landing for ferries crossing the river between Saugerties and the village of Tivoli. One can see Swan House shimmering in the landscape from the edge of Rose Hill, the Marden family’s 19th-century Tivoli estate.

The Depression, along with the advent of more efficient modes of transport, scuppered the last of the large ships landing at Long Dock in the early 1930s, but ferries continued to make the two-minute trip across the water until 1938. After that, the structure was decommissioned from professional service and sold, becoming the only privately owned peninsula on the Hudson. The Mardens purchased the property in 2011, but it took a full decade before they engaged designer Daniel Sachs and architect Kevin Lindores of the AD100 firm Sachs Lindores Architecture, Interiors to execute a full-scale renovation.

The primary bath features custom zellige tiles, a vintage Vistosi chandelier, an antique marble sink, and a tub by The Water Monopoly.

Sachs Lindores remodeled the entry with a windscreen of glass brick. The chair is by Gaetano Pesce.

Yellow zellige tiles meet a pale pink Aga range beneath a custom zinc hood in the kitchen. The pendant light is by Adolf Loos from WOKA.

Brice Marden’s For Helen – Valentine 2019 (2015–18) hangs on the black-tiled fireplace tower that mediates the bedroom and living room.

A custom bed is flanked by an antique French console table and a Charles Rohlfs hall chair. Lighting includes a Franz West chandelier and a floor lamp by Achille and Pier Giacomo Castiglioni.

“Early on we demolished a few walls to open up the views, but it was pretty raw. We’d just go over and watch the boats go by,” Helen recalls. “You have a completely different relationship with the river when you’re sitting in the middle of it.”

Given the famously cultivated, idiosyncratic tastes of the homeowners, the collaboration between Sachs Lindores and their clients was unusually fertile. Together, they reimagined the derelict building as a trick box for trapping the natural light that bounces off the water on all sides, with reflective, lead-coated copper siding and a zinc roof on the exterior and fields of luminous plaster, tile, and marble within. “Helen never shies away from a bold gesture. At first, she told us to paint the house red, but when we presented the idea of a glistening metal-clad box with light dancing on the skin, she immediately went for it,” Sachs recalls. “Brice and Helen were very interconnected in their aesthetic tastes and decision making,” Lindores adds. “As you might imagine, they studied every paint color and trim detail.”

Ruins of the 19th-century dock remain alongside the house.

A guest room is outfitted with a Pierre Jeanneret daybed, lounge chairs by Monika Mulder for IKEA, a vintage Kevin Walz standing lamp, and a Mathieu Matégot magazine rack. Painting by Helen Marden.

Sigmar Polke’s Untitled (1998) hangs above a vintage Walter Knoll sofa in the first-floor sitting room.

While retaining the shape of its original architectural envelope, the house was essentially rebuilt, with new window configurations, open circulation, and an exposed ceiling, all in service of maximizing watery vistas and ease of use. On the lofty upper level, the existing chimney, newly revealed in its full floor-to-ceiling height, was clad in glossy black brick tile. The monolithic form now feels like a high altar in a temple of light. Custom zellige tiles imported from Fez cover the walls of the kitchen and baths, where Helen’s genius for juxtaposing colors and materials comes into high relief.

The polyglot ensemble of furnishings hews closely to the signature Marden mix: Moroccan rugs; bold contemporary designs by the likes of Gaetano Pesce, Marcel Wanders, and the Campana Brothers; humble American folk pieces; 20th-century classics by Paavo Tynell, Adolf Loos, and Pierre Jeanneret; and a few Continental antiques to leaven the brew. “I just pick things that I like, things that make me happy,” Helen says, pooh-poohing the idea of some grand decorative vision. Her designers would demur. “She has an incredible eye,” Sachs insists. “The more crazy Helen would get, the more Brice liked it.”

#4844. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.
