#4843. What Does It Really Mean to Be Fit for Your Age? My Mom and I Put It to the Test at the Super Age Games

These eight fitness challenges allegedly predict how long and well you’ll live.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

What if you could predict your healthspan? That’s the idea behind the Super Age Games, which bills itself as “the world’s first live longevity fitness competition,” helping participants gauge how long they’ll live well.

The games (which took place this year in New York City on November 7) are centered around eight trials testing markers that predict longevity: grip strength, aerobic capacity, agility, balance, functional strength, memory, and relational capacity. Anyone could sign up and compete throughout the day with a thousand other athletes. There was an overall winner, a team competition winner, and winners within each age group for women and men. But also, all participants received a medal and a report outlining their strengths and areas of improvement, as well as personalized longevity training tips.

This fall, the creators behind the Super Age media brand hosted a practice day in NYC where anyone could attend and be the first to test-run the trials. My mom—who’s been interested in all things health and wellness since she was my age (I’m 26, she’s now 64). She happened to be visiting me in the city that weekend, so she signed us up.

Even as lifelong gym rats, after we experienced the tests, we both realized there are key areas of training that our workout routines are missing. Here’s what the competition taught us about our overall health—and what we can work on to live stronger for longer.

As we walked into the venue, the Metropolitan Pavilion, we noticed cones, obstacles to jump over, balance beams, and air bikes sitting on hardwood floor spread throughout the room into different stations. I felt like I was right back in elementary school taking on a field-day-meets-presidential-physical-fitness-test challenge.

There appeared to be people of all ages there—people younger than me, up to those in their 70s—and an even split between women and men. Some people came to practice day because they got the invite from being on the Super Age newsletter mailing list and wanted to try it out, while others came because they were competing at the real event in November.

My mom and I didn’t train for the specific challenges beyond our general fitness routines (a few days a week of strength training and cardio), so we weren’t sure how we would fare. However, there was time to practice each station before the actual games started—so we explored the balance beam and obstacle course.

After all of the participants arrived and everyone settled in, we were split into groups and began each trial in a specific order. We had to wait a bit to begin, and there was also a bit of downtime in between each trial as we waited for room to open up on the equipment. While the trials themselves were timed, the time in between the trials wasn’t, so we could take our time a bit and catch our breath.

The goal of each trial was different: Some were to be completed as fast as possible, or as slow as possible, while some were based on data like getting your highest VO2 max. After the practice day, we received an email of our scores, which were adjusted based on age and sex, and compared us against the other 50 athletes who participated. (During the actual Super Age Games, though, the data field was much larger.)

The email also included an action plan recommending how we could improve each of our scores. The feedback came from the work they’ve done with the Buck Institute for Research on Aging, performance coach Andy Walshe, PhD, and their head trainer, as well as longevity research and expert interviews, according to Heather Hurlock, founding editor at Super Age.

The challenge: Jump over and crawl under four gates set 10 meters apart as fast as possible to test agility, explosive movement, and gait speed, which research shows are predictors of how long you’ll live.

At first glance, my mom and I were both intimidated by the plywood box (about 2.5 feet tall) we had to jump over. It took a second to figure out how to jump over the box because everyone did it differently, but eventually, we got into the swing of things. My mom and I took off in a running start, maintained our speed throughout as we jumped over the boxes and slid under the ropes, and agreed that the challenge wasn’t that hard, and in fact, we both really enjoyed it! (However, we did end up with a few bruises from hitting the boxes and floor pretty hard.)

I finished in 80 seconds, while my mom finished in 73. (Go, mom!) Our feedback—formed from the research that Super Age has done—told us that our agility is above average.

To get better at moving quickly over and under obstacles, add in jumping exercises like directional hops and line drills, before more advanced exercises such as lateral shuffles and single-leg hop overs. These drills will help grow your coordination, balance, and power skills, as well as spatial awareness. Plus, these moves will increase your lateral quickness and help develop foot speed—all important for helping prevent falls as you grow older.

The challenge: Complete a six-minute memory game from NeuroTracker, a cognitive training tool, on computers to focus on cognitive capacity under load. Keep track of a specific set of balls moving across the screen and identify them seconds later as the speed of the balls increases.

My mom and I found that the longer the game went on, the harder it was, because we’re so used to looking at short-form content all day, so it was hard to keep focus. We couldn’t take our eyes (or mind) off of the screen for even a second, or else we were screwed for that round. (But hey, at least I know it was good for my brain.) My mom got a near-perfect score, while I had some room to grow.

Take your aerobic exercise seriously, which has been associated with improved cognitive function in older adults, suggests Aashaun Khedaru, exercise physiologist supervisor at the Sports Performance Center at NYU Langone Health. The Super Age feedback recommended walking briskly for 30 minutes, three to five times a week, to boost blood flow to the brain, and pairing it with memory or reaction games.

The challenge: Walk forward and then backward on a 12-foot balance beam carrying a 10-lb hydro training tube filled with water, front-racked, in as few steps as possible—without stepping off—to gauge balance and stability.

This trial was my personal favorite, and the one I felt most confident on (possibly due to six years of classical ballet training). There was a learning curve to just holding the tube—it could easily throw you off balance. But I just had to move slowly and keep my focus straight ahead and slightly down. I scored lower than I thought I would, though, with 49 steps, because I thought the goal was to just not fall off—not to take the smallest amount of steps possible.

For my mom, though, this one was more challenging, especially the part where we walked backward with the hydro tube. She said the level of coordination it required almost felt like trying to catch a ball while balancing on one leg. But when she engaged her core, walking the beam became easier. (She even scored better than me, finishing in 30 steps!)

The Super Age Games feedback recommended standing on one leg for 30 seconds per side each day, then trying it with our eyes closed, and adding some lunges and single-leg deadlifts into our routines. (We already do!)

Lunges can improve muscle function and balance because they isolate the quads and work your range of motion, according to a small study that had middle-aged women do eight weeks of lunge exercises to better their lower extremity strength and balance. Single-leg deadlifts can increase muscular strength and balance since it puts you in an unstable position, per a 2026 study in Scientific Reports that had 30 men perform the exercise on unstable surfaces to see if it limited joint mobility and strength gains.

The challenge: Pedal at an all-out effort on an assault bike for four minutes to earn your highest VO2 max, which is the maximum amount of oxygen your body can hold during exercise. The better your VO2 max is, the more efficiently your body produces energy, which means better endurance and stamina.

This trial carries the most weight in the overall score, Hurlock says—and the games’ creators warned it would be the toughest. My mom agreed: It was straight-up “just hard,” she said. After three grueling trials, the thought of going all out on the assault bike for four minutes was less than appealing. So, we both held back for most of it, though I kicked things into high gear for the final minute.

My score was pretty average, while my mom fared slightly better. But according to Khedaru, this four-minute challenge wasn't the most accurate way to measure VO2 max. For a more precise reading, you'd typically undergo a longer, supervised treadmill test in a lab. Fitness wearables like Apple Watches and Fitbits can also estimate VO2 max using workout data.

Your VO2 max will depend on your age and workouts, but this chart depicts where you should aim to be, based on your age:

My action plan said to do brisk walks or easy cycling to build toward HIIT, while my mom’s plan recommended adding one weekly 4x4 session to her routine: four minutes hard, then three easy, four times through. (I already run for about 90 minutes every week and do some light zone 2 work, so I feel pretty good in the cardio department.) But you can also walk or run on an incline and eventually do longer cardio sessions (45 minutes to an hour at a conversational pace) to improve your endurance. Aim for two to four cardio workouts per week.

The challenge: Crawl across a 40-foot cargo net as fast as possible to gauge functional strength and coordination.

We felt like little kids again, climbing over the net like we were back on an elementary school playground. It also tested the most aspects of longevity, in our opinion: coordination, core strength, upper-body strength, flexibility, mobility, and mental focus. I was feeling a bit lightheaded at this point in the trials (probably because it required me to be bent over crawling and I hadn’t eaten much that day), so it was harder than I thought it would be. It took my mom a second to get into a rhythm and figure out where to place her hands and feet, but once she did, she enjoyed it.

I completed the challenge in 69 seconds while my mom finished in 115 seconds (almost two minutes).

To improve functional strength and coordination, Khedaru recommends targeting the posterior chain (the backside of your body) through a mix of upper- and lower-body compound movements, which work multiple muscles. Think shoulder presses, pull-ups, lateral pulldowns, and farmer’s carries, since most of your body weight will be on your arms and shoulders. But you can also add some step-ups into your routine as well since crawling involves some leg work too; other functional leg exercises include squats, deadlifts, lunges, and calf raises, WH previously wrote. All of these exercises will build strength in your hamstrings, glutes, quads, and calves.

The challenge: Dead hang on a bar for as long as you can to test grip strength, one of the biggest predictors of longevity.

I consider myself to have a decent amount of upper-body strength, but dead hangs are still challenging. On my mom’s part, she got a shoulder replacement two years ago, so she’s had to build her shoulder strength from the ground up, particularly with hangs. (Thankfully, they let us use chalk, which can absorb sweat and moisture and make it easier to grip the bar.)

We both hung for over a minute each, which was far longer than we’d hung in practice at the gym, so we were very happy with our times. According to Khedaru, that’s good too: He says women in their 20s and 30s should be able to hang for over 70 seconds, while those in their 40s to 60s should be able to hold 45 seconds.

You can practice hanging, but also lean on farmer’s carries and kettlebell swings so your hands practice holding heavy weight and improving that grip strength.

The challenge: Complete two exercises on an iPad game to test your emotional intelligence, as research shows that those with stronger social relationships live longer. First, stare at a neutral face, then identify an emotional face that flashes on screen for two-tenths of a second (anger, contempt, surprise, happiness, etc.); eventually the faces will be shown for a shorter period, one-tenth of a second. Next, choose how you’d respond to five real-life scenarios where conflict is involved. Example: “Someone cuts in front of you with the airport line and you're going to miss your flight. Do you call them out on it or do you let it go because it's not worth it?”

The first exercise felt extremely difficult because we were already physically and mentally fatigued from the previous trials; the emotions blinked so quickly that you could barely tell which facial features had changed. So, I feel like I didn’t do as well as I wanted—especially because I was already so mentally fatigued. However, the second exercise went way better; it was pretty easy for us to pick which ones were the “correct” answers. (Honestly, it reminded me of those HR training situational videos that you have to complete for work every year.)

I didn’t get the best score on this one, which would’ve come with getting the most answers right, but my mom totally crushed it.

For stronger social skills, don’t be afraid to practice making new friends. Reach out in a way that feels natural for you—in person, text, DM—then choose an activity that sounds fun, but simple, like coffee or lunch, WH previously reported. Feel free to reach out to mutual friends first, if speaking to a stranger feels a bit intimidating.

The challenge: Run (or walk) 800 meters (nearly half a mile) carrying a sandbag weighing 10, 25, 40, or 50 pounds to test both grip strength and the cardiovascular system.

Unfortunately, we didn’t get to try this one because it was rainy and slippery outside—but we weren’t too disappointed, because we were tired. Still, Khedaru says that for 20- and 30-year-olds, your goal should be to carry 25 percent of your total body weight and complete the challenge in under 5 minutes. Those who are older should be able to carry 15 to 25 percent of their body weight and finish in around 6 minutes.

Khedaru says to regularly train your aerobic capacity and lift weights, specifically through exercises like farmer’s carries and walking lunges.

In fact, having a healthy balance of both aerobic and resistance training will help you in all of these challenges—which will translate to real-life longevity, Khedaru says. Make sure you’re regularly doing both low- and high-intensity cardiovascular work, as well as increasing reps, sets, and weight when you resistance train—a principle known as progressive overload.

The games were harder than we thought. Each activity by itself wasn’t too difficult, but by the time we completed all of them back to back and in a specific order, we were totally wiped out physically and mentally. For instance, the Over Under required a lot of energy and agility right off the bat, then we had to go right into the Synapse, which required a lot of mental focus. By the time we got to challenge number four—The Inferno—we both felt like we could’ve used a bit of a break. That’s why after The Sync, another challenge that used mental focus, we were fine to skip the last challenge, which required running with a heavy sandbag. It was clearly designed to be a total mental, emotional, and physical workout.

In fact, my hardest events were The Synapse and The Sync—and they certainly weren’t made easier after completing serious physical challenges. On the flip side, my mom crushed both of those challenges at 64, and it makes sense: She’s whip-smart, regularly works out, and stays on top of her brain health.

That said, at 26, I want to start strengthening my cognitive abilities now. While I work out regularly—and that does help my brain health some—I could probably play more brain and memory games (even when I’m tired) and scroll a little bit less on Instagram to lengthen my attention span. (Something my mom doesn’t do.)

Neither The Over Under nor The Net were our best events (especially the latter because it was one of the last events and we were tired). Both trials required mobility, agility, speed, and power in movements that we don’t really practice day to day: jumping and sliding over a high obstacle, and crawling over an unsteady net. But at 64, my mom was really happy that she could finish them (in great time, might I add!). For me, I’m a recreational runner and regularly do HIIT and speed work, so I felt good about my power and speed. But I could probably integrate more crawls and mobility work into my routine.

Ultimately, performing each of the eight challenges made us look differently at how we work out and live our day-to-day lives. Now, we have a good idea of our fitness and wellness strengths—and weaknesses—which will help inform our future workout and wellness habits.

In her 60s, my mom wants to do more agility, speed, and power work. As a kid, you run around, balance, hang, jump, and climb all the time, but as adults, you tend to stay more linear. Then, you naturally lose those skills because you’re not using them. So, completing this practice day made her want to try more of these challenges on a regular basis, instead of always taking the easy way through life.

For me, I’m much more motivated to be wary of and work on my long-term brain health and mental endurance. Maybe that looks like going for a run, and then playing brain and memory games instead of scrolling on Instagram.

Addison Aloian is the associate health & fitness editor at Women’s Health, where she writes and edits across the health, weight loss, and fitness verticals. #4842. When Grief Lies Just Below the Surface

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

In dealing with the recent passing of her grandmother, Aleh's reaction remained distanced, somehow removed. Yet when she dreamed of the death of an online acquaintance, and especially upon analyzing her dream, she was able to break through the disconnection and bring her feelings to the surface.

I met a woman last year, Autumn, who I communicate back and forth with online. Her brother Tobias passed away recently from health complications.

In this dream, I was excited to see her, since it had been so long and I felt the need to give her a big hug. I didn't get a chance to attend the funeral, so in my dreams, I told her I was so very sorry and that we will also miss him. It was a mixed feeling of happiness to see her, while also helping her grieve.

I wondered, "When did you have this dream?"

"Did you know Autumn's brother? It sounds like you did."

"No," Aleh said, "I didn't get the chance to meet him."

I added, "I'm curious about how you said you've known Autumn for a year but you 'communicate back and forth online.' You don’t see her in person?"

Aleh explained, "No, not anymore. We wanted to hang out, but with our busy schedules it’s been hard to plan anything. I've known Autumn for a year."

I suggested, "You mentioned that you had 'mixed feelings' in your dream. Can you think of a recent circumstance in your life you have 'mixed' feelings about, perhaps even a mix of happiness and grief?"

Aleh exclaimed, "My grandma passed away this past Sunday! I didn’t see her much the last few months because I knew it was coming. I've been a lot closer and communicating more with my parents. My dad's mom was the one who passed.

"I tend to remember more dreams after grief, it seems."

I said, "Perhaps Tobias’ appearance in your dream reflects your not seeing your grandmother in the months before she passed on. Why do you say you didn’t see her much 'because you knew it was coming'? Were you close with your dad’s mom?"

Aleh acknowledged, "I wasn't as close with her as I was with my grandpa growing up. I had a feeling it was almost time for her to pass away and wanted to keep her memory as someone very smiley and talkative. It didn't occur to me that Tobias appearing in the dream reflects me not seeing my grandmother. That really fits!"

I continued, "Let's investigate the two people who appear in your dream. Tell me, please, what comes to mind about Autumn's personality. What about Tobias? What do you know about him? Did you ever have a conversation with Tobias? Was he a friend too?"

Aleh offered, "Autumn is very happy. She has a great sense of humor and is always cracking jokes. I did have a conversation with Tobias online. He enjoyed conversations with many people online, giving motivational advice. He was also nice and very positive."

I reflected on Aleh's words. "Both your dream and your waking-life situation bring to mind matters involving death and funerals. Yet I'm struck by the light, happy tone of the words you're using: 'very smiley and talkative,' 'very happy,' 'motivational and positive.' You mentioned feeling a mix of happiness and grief, but I'm not hearing much grief.

"Does this observation ring true for you?"

Aleh responded, "I honestly didn't think about whether I've been feeling grief until you mentioned about my answers just now being pretty 'light.' I have to reflect on this. Now, I can also see that the characters in my dream aren't people I connect with on an everyday basis. They're nice, but I don't feel very connected to them."

I asked, "Does this lack of connection in your dream mirror any of your feelings in your waking-life situation?"

Aleh answered aloud and thoughtfully, "Am I really not grieving, or do I really not feel sad from my grandmother's passing? Am I so disconnected? No, I do feel sad, but what hurts me more is trying to be there for my parents. Especially my dad, who just lost his mom."

Making a clearer connection, she added, "Am I trying to comfort my own self in this dream? Omg I am, and I want to cry now. Finally."

The dream is Aleh's vehicle to comfort herself. In addition, by putting herself in a place where she's reaching out to someone who is grieving but who she feels less "connected" to than her own dad, she's giving herself some space to feel her own grief.

Additionally, we can see from this dream interpretation how important it is to pay attention to the words that the dreamer says when talking about all aspects of the analysis, not only while discussing the dream itself but also all associations with the dream. The precise words the dreamer uses during different parts of the discussion can often bring to the surface the emotional aspects of their waking-life situation that they are pushing below the surface.

#4841. Fall Weddings Are More Popular Than Ever. Here's How to Dress for One (The Right Way)

Autumn is now the most popular season to tie the knot.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WEDDINGS CAN be hard to dress for, and this isn’t limited to those directly involved; being a mere attendant requires some degree of planning. I’ve attended quite a few weddings over the last year, both as a groomsman and as a regular guest, both with their own sartorial challenges. (I actually found it more stressful not being in the wedding party, at least in one aspect: I had to pick out my own outfit. This also allowed for a little creativity.)

I covered some options for summer weddings a few months back, and just like that, we’re on to the next season. Fall has arguably become the season for weddings; in fact, October recently overtook June as the most popular month for weddings in the U.S. I can attest to this; I was in two separate ones last October.

Summer and fall weddings have quite a few differences. You can get away with some more “fun” looks in the summer, and you can get a little more creative with the materials (linen, seersucker, etc.). Fall weddings are typically a little more buttoned-up, but there’s a little wiggle room there, too.

I’ll go through some of the easiest ways for guys to dress for an autumn affair—with different wedding types in mind—to get you off the ground. We also included plenty of price points because, as everyone knows, weddings can get expensive fast.

Brooks Brothers Explorer Collection Non-Iron Twill Button Down Collar

Cole Haan Men's Grand Neoclassic Plain Toe Oxfords

We’ll start with what we consider a traditional wedding: a separate ceremony at a church, chapel, or the wedding venue without a black-tie dress code. This is about as classic as it gets, so you don’t have to go overboard—but we do recommend wearing a timeless suit. Our style team has tested plenty of affordable menswear brands offering solid options that approximate the look and fit of made-to-measure tailoring. One of them is the Black Tux, an upstart that offers suits for both rental and purchase, with virtual and in-person fittings to match you with the closest standard size. The prices are great, too: the Essential Suit is just under $300 all in. We also happened to score a 20 percent off code for the Black Tux, made exclusively for Men’s Health readers. Just use code MH20 at checkout (minimum of $295). The code’s good until October 31. Most of its higher-priced suits also include a rental option, but for the extra $100 or so, we’d recommend just buying one. The True Navy is a safe color you can wear year-round. The Grey Suit is a step up and is made from a heavier—but still breathable—merino wool. Perfect for the autumn temperatures.

A classic dress shirt is more than okay, but if you want to stand out in an otherwise pretty basic look, you can go with a classic twill dress shirt like this one from Brooks Brothers. You can get a little bit more creative with the tie, but nothing too crazy; the left-to-right diagonal stripes of a classic rep tie keep it distinguished. A Classic Textured Solid Tie is always a safe bet, too. Baby blue and pink go well with a gray suit, and navy, black, and red look better with gray. The shoes are easy, too: black plain-toe oxfords for grays, and these simple brown Astorflex Loafers with a crisp navy blue.

Brooks Brothers Classic Fit Double-Breasted Wool Pinstripe 1818 Suit

Charles Tyrwhitt Cotton Pocket Square - White

Mack Weldon Silver Extended Crew Dress Sock

The Black Tux Picture Frame Brushed Gold Tie Bar

Black-tie affairs probably require even less creativity, but there are definitely ways to push the envelope to stand out. The safe choice, of course, is the classic tux. If you plan to need one on multiple occasions, we also love that the Black Tux once again gets top marks; its Essential option is also under $300. There are some pricier options you can also rent, but the Essential Tux is low-key enough to rock at any formal occasion. SuitShop is another upstart offering ready-to-wear tuxedos at accessible prices, including several options under $300. Accessories-wise, you can opt for a super fancy pair of onyx cufflinks from one of our favorite watch brands, Shinola, but something a little more budget-friendly is more than okay.

Nowadays, you don’t have to go all-black, at least depending on the event. But if you do deviate, you'd better make it count. Like upgrading to a double-breasted suit, for example. The Classic Fit Double-Breasted Wool Pinstripe 1818 Suit elevates your look without making you look like a Prohibition-era mobster (surprisingly, a very fine line).

The other big component of all of this: your shoes. You probably don’t want to go with a loafer; an oxford or derby shoe is the better option. Our favorite: Cole Haan’s Hawthorne Oxfords, a classic dress shoe that’s made with the brand’s famously comfortable insoles so your dogs will stay happy for hours. It’s also versatile enough to wear at dressy events or in a more casual office vibe. In other words, you’ll be getting a lot of use out of it.

If you want to go all out, you can go full custom. Go big or go home, as they say. If you’re in the NYC area, Alan David Custom is a great choice. The bespoke tailor will give you a sample suit to try on before making final decisions, and the experience is a throwback to classier times. They’ll even ship it to you when it’s all said and done. If you want to go fully custom, you’ll also need the shoes to match.

Bonobos Empire Stretch Italian Wool Tuxedo

Todd Snyder Italian Lightweight Sutton Jacket

Quince Supima Cotton Herringbone Dress Shirt

Todd Snyder Relaxed Fit Japanese Selvedge Chino

Reigning Champ Stretch Chino Marina Standard Pant

Allen Edmonds Rhett Cap-toe Oxford Dress Shoe

Cocktail weddings give you a little more freedom than a traditional one. Here, you can rock a classic suit or a nice blazer and slacks, and you wouldn’t be wrong either way. The classic Ludlow tux from J.Crew gives off serious old-school cocktail jacket vibes, and it’s reserved for swankier occasions. Todd Snyder’s Italian Lightweight Sutton Jacket is another high-end option that’s both breathable and easy to wear throughout the night. If you wear blazers regularly, you’ll also get plenty of use out of this, even into the hotter months. Todd Snyder also makes our favorite pair of relaxed-fit chinos that check a lot of boxes for us. The Relaxed Fit Japanese Selvedge Chino is a steep departure from the ones we wear to the office, which is why it’s such a legit option for dressier occasions.

If the baggier fit (and higher price tag) is scaring you off a bit, Reigning Champ makes an ultra-breathable cotton-twill chino that wears more like a standard dress pant. They’re comfortable, breathable, and have a little added stretch; you’ll get a lot of use out of them outside the wedding. The other big component of all of this: your shoes. You probably don’t want to go with a loafer; an Oxford or derby shoe is the better option. Our style team loves Allen Edmonds’. It’s made with calfskin leather, with a surprisingly light-yet-cushioned outsole that’s comfortable enough to use all night.

Billy Reid Exploded Glen Plaid Archie Jacket

Brooks Brothers Straight-Fit Cotton Advantage Chino Pants

Brooks Brothers Friday Shirt, Oxford Patterns

Madewell Johnny-Collar Sweater Polo in Slub Knit Cotton

Cole Haan Zerogrand Remastered Wing Tip Oxford

Barns have since had a huge come-up and are now a hugely popular wedding venue. Regardless of your stance on barn weddings, you have to dress a little differently. Vineyard weddings (and really any outdoor event) live in that same category. If you’re looking at a late-fall event, you’ll want something a little warmer. The Grey Plaid Wool Suit is a step up in that department without being too overbearing; the subtle designs also scream fall. You can also go with the blazer-and-dress-pants route. Abercrombie’s A&F Collins Blazer is a fantastic budget option, and the Olive Stripe colorway similarly gives off fall vibes. It’s easy to pair with dressier chinos, like the Straight-Fit Cotton Advantage Chino Pants from Brooks Brothers. They’re essentially dress pants with a certain chinoesque comfort.

If you do go this route, you can have a little fun with the undershirt; Brooks Brothers’ Friday Shirt can add some flair to your getup. Madewell’s Johnny-Collar Sweater Polo is also a nice departure from your traditional button-down (and a lot more comfortable, too). If the wedding isn’t all that fancy, you can get away with rocking some of the most comfortable dress shoes/sneakers out there: Cole Haan’s Zerogrand Remastered Wing Tip Oxfords.

Buck Mason Capitola Linen Carry-On Jacket

Bonobos Stretch Weekday Warrior Dress Pants

Reigning Champ Heavyweight Jersey OG T-Shirt

The destination wedding can definitely be a challenge, depending on how close you are to the person (or people) getting married. They’re always a great time, though, and you can get similarly creative. We suggest a travel blazer; you’re already shelling out a lot of money for flights and accommodations, so you can save a few bucks by not checking a full suit. Our style director, Christian Gollayan, recently did a full review of the Bonobos Jetsetter Knit Blazer. He described it as a “lifesaver” when traveling. You can definitely rock it at a fall destination wedding, especially considering the hardworking knit construction. For a lighter, beachy vibe, Buck Mason’s Capitola Linen Carry-On Jacket is my own go-to. It holds its shape well for linen, and some of the darker colors work well for any season.

Pants are easy to pack, so we’d suggest going with something that helps you stand out. The Bonobos Stretch Weekday Warrior Dress Pants are the perfect counterpart to the Jetsetter, and you can wear them around the office when you’re not in wedding mode. The Italian Linen Sutton Trousers are a luxury pick, and the white colorway pairs particularly well with a navy blazer for a classic look. They’re also a lot easier to pack than regular dress pants. If the destination wedding is beach-themed, you can even get away with rocking a tee underneath your blazer. You don’t want to go with something too casual, and the Heavyweight Jersey OG T-Shirt from Reigning Champ is anything but. It’s well-made, fits like a glove, and is a great way to show off some jewelry if you like to wear a chain or two.

#4840. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4838. How Can We Stop Sexual Violence?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

I didn’t just start thinking about how to end sexual violence when I sat down to write this. I’ve been thinking about it for most of my life, certainly since adolescence, when people began confiding in me about the assaults that devastated them. One friend described what happened to them as a slow murder of their soul.

I think about everyone who stayed silent out of shame or fear. I think about those who did speak out and were blamed or not believed by their communities, their families, and their friends, the very people who were supposed to support and advocate for them. Many described this secondary assault as more painful than the first.

So when I read about the alleged gang rape at Cornell, I felt deep sorrow for Jane Doe and shock at the response of the men and women who spoke out against her. We must not forget that sexual assault is never the victim’s fault. Responsibility always belongs to the person who assaults them. It does not matter what she wore, what her relationship was with the person or people who assaulted her, or whether she said yes and then changed her mind. And if she was under the influence of substances, even by her own choice, that does not lessen anyone else’s responsibility. I am speaking as a clinician and as a human, not as a lawyer.

So how do we teach our children, especially our sons, not to sexually assault another person?

That question keeps haunting me. I don’t know the men involved in the Cornell case, or the other countless men who have committed sexual assault. I do know that what was taught, or not taught, to them before the assaults contributed to their behavior — for instance, when they ignored a person telling them “No,” either verbally or by their body language; when belonging to a group mattered more than doing what was right; when they disregarded a person’s boundary; when they did not stop when a person was impaired; or when they did not protect a person in danger, and all of this was seen as acceptable.

I couldn’t help but look back at my own children’s childhoods. Some of my proudest moments as a mother happened at parent-teacher conferences when I learned that my son had noticed a classmate sitting alone and invited him to join his lunch table. Another time, I learned that my daughter had stood up for a child who was being bullied, knowing it might cost her friendships.

We begin shaping our children the moment we hold them as infants and respond to their needs with love and compassion. Babies learn empathy by receiving it when we respond to their cries and name their feelings. They learn that their feelings matter, as do the feelings of others. How we treat our children and others becomes how they treat other people as well.

We teach toddlers about boundaries by teaching them that their bodies belong to them. That means not forcing them to hug relatives, and making sure that when a sibling says “stop,” they stop. And we teach them that behavior has consequences: When you hurt someone, you take responsibility for what you did and do what you can to make the situation better.

Children learn respect, compassion, and right from wrong through what their parents (or primary caregivers) say, how they behave, and what they overhear. If they hear the adults around them say a girl “asked for it,” that is where victim-blaming is learned. Instead, we can model kindness, empathy, respect for boundaries, respect for others, self-respect, respect for rules, and the critical thinking it takes to resist groupthink.

We can’t control every influence. Children learn from everything around them: school, friends, their friends’ parents, television, and social media. That is why parents’ influence is so important. Their words and actions matter. Parenting happens through both messaging and modeling. Children notice more than most parents realize: the subtle cues and the conversations they assume their children weren’t paying attention to. And when a parent does realize that they sent the wrong message through words or behavior, they can tell their children they made a mistake and explain what they want them to learn instead.

Through our own actions, we show children how to respect other people’s boundaries and needs. We teach them to read one another’s facial expressions and body language. We teach them that if someone has been drinking or using other substances and is not able to make decisions for themselves, they cannot take advantage of that person. We teach them that wrongdoing has consequences. And we teach them that if they are part of a group that is doing things they are uncomfortable with, or that they know are wrong, they need to separate from the group and even get help if needed. Being different from a group is hard, but doing what’s right matters more.

Teaching empathy, compassion, boundaries, respect, courage, ethics, consequences, and critical thinking is no guarantee against abuse, but it’s certainly a great start. And I hope that raising children with empathy means raising adults who believe survivors and provide support.

#4835. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

#4834. How to Overcome Retirement Anxiety

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

The decision to leave the workforce is bittersweet for some and exciting for others—who have been literally counting the days, and even hours, until the jail gate swings open. But when the day comes and goes, after the retirement party is over, the anxiety remains. This phenomenon, which is unexpected for many recent retirees, lingers over time. Fortunately, it has a name, an explanation, and a solution. Research explains.

Tarani Chandola et al. (2025) investigated the cause of what they term “anxious Mondays” in 3511 older adults aged 50 or older living in England.[i] They discovered a link between Monday anxiety and higher cortisol levels measured through hair samples; they did not find significant differences in cortisol levels produced by anxiety on other days of the week. Interestingly, regarding retirees, Chandola and team found that both working and nonworking older adults experience Monday anxiety, proving the phenomenon is tied to the start of the week rather than employment.

Regarding Mondays, the researchers also recognize it the day as linked with higher levels of cardiovascular disease events, with a 19 percent increase in confirmed myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac deaths, a statistic found in both men and women both above and below age 65. They also recognize the “Monday blues” effect on mood, highlighting the psychological effects of beginning the work week. Regarding cortisol levels, Chandola and colleagues explain that stress triggers the nervous system to activate a physiological process that increases cortisol levels.

Interpreting their results, Chandola and team conclude that the Monday effect reflects the reality that although most people adapt to Monday anxiety over their working life, not everyone adjusts. Some people continue to experience the effect after they retire.

Tarani Chandola and Benjamin Becker noted that one reason Mondays may be stressful for both working and nonworking adults is the uncertainty that accompanies the start of the workweek; another is that the Monday effect may become an automatic response and persist even after retirement, shaped through decades of routine.[ii]

Regardless of the explanation, finding a solution to Monday blues may improve quality of life both physically and emotionally. One way to address the issue is to replace the dread and uncertainty of a coming week by planning it instead.

Counteracting ingrained patterns of thinking and behaving in anticipation of the week's start may be easier when addressing both thoughts and behavior. Intentionally planning enjoyable activities on Monday may counteract the stress previously associated with the uncertainty and anxiety of the workweek. Here are some ideas.

Connecting with retired colleagues. Share the enjoyment of being free from workplace demands with a former co-worker in your same situation. Joining a group of retirees within your industry or area of expertise can provide a robust social life that carries forth the meaning behind your career choice, without the daily stress.

Reconnecting with faith, family, and friends. Retirement is a unique opportunity to recapture the joy of experiencing what you missed for so many years—relationships. Plan Mondays as a day to schedule coveted family time, and meet with people you haven’t seen or spoken to when you were “too busy.”

Rescheduling Monday. Counteract the ingrained emotional reaction to an unpredictable week and schedule an enjoyable Monday morning activity to replace uncertainty with pleasure; coffee with a friend, a walk on the beach with your spouse, or a road trip bucket-list adventure gives you something exciting to look forward to. Ideally designed to replace the stress and anxiety of an unpredictable week, pre-scheduling Monday will also help prevent the “Sunday blues” that often foreshadow the morning to come.

Ideally, the plan is to enjoy retirement every day of the week, as you have the luxury of planning the best years of your life.

[i] Tarani Chandola, Wanying Ling, Patrick Rouxel, “Are anxious Mondays associated with HPA-axis dysregulation? A longitudinal study of older adults in England,” Journal of Affective Disorders, Volume 389, 2025, 119611.

#4833. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4832. Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Air: Which New Fitbit Should You Buy?

Do you want a less distracting tracker or one with a screen and built-in GPS?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

GOOGLE DIDN’T RELEASE a major new Fitbit fitness tracker for two and a half years after the Charge 6 came out in October 2023. Then it released two new models in five months. The first, the $99 Fitbit Air, came out in May and works a lot like a Whoop. You wear it day and night, and it sends your heart rate, sleep, and workout data to the Google Health app on your phone.Second is the $179 Fitbit Edge, which followed in October as the Charge 6’s successor. It offers the same features as the Air and adds a 1.34-inch screen, built-in GPS, and an ECG app that checks your heart rhythm for signs of atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises your stroke risk. Both trackers pair with iPhones and Android phones, so neither is exclusive to Google’s platform.For most people, deciding between them comes down to one question: do you want to see your pace and heart rate on your wrist during a workout, or are you fine checking everything on your phone afterward?

With no screen and no buttons, the Fitbit Air is as simple as they come to use. Google rates its battery at up to seven days, so you won’t have to charge every night. It’s also the cheaper way to get Google’s Health Coach. The $99 price includes three free months of Google’s Health Premium, which costs $9.99 a month after that.The Fitbit Edge shows your pace and heart rate on its screen during a workout, and its built-in GPS records your route without your phone. If you run or ride outdoors, you can leave your phone at home and still come back with a map and split times. The Edge also has two sensors the Air doesn’t: electrical sensors for the ECG app, and an altimeter that measures elevation gain on a hike and counts the floors you climb. It costs $80 more than the Air, and turning on its always-on display cuts the battery from about seven days to about two.

The Air’s tracker module is a 1.37 x 0.66-inch pod, and it’s about 25 percent smaller than the discontinued Fitbit Luxe. The pod pops out of its band and snaps into another one in a few seconds, so you can wear the fabric Performance Loop to sleep and switch to the silicone Active Band for a sweaty workout. If you want something dressier, the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band and a new Metal Mesh band are also available.The Edge measures 1.54 x 1.01 inches and is almost half an inch thick, with a pill-shaped body that’s noticeably larger than the Air. A side button opens the app list and takes you back to the clock face. It comes in Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon, with six band styles that run from the sweat-resistant Active Sport Band to a Metal Links bracelet. Both trackers are rated IP68 and 5ATM, which means they have dust and water protection.

The Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge record the same health data. Both measure your heart rate around the clock, plus blood oxygen, overnight skin temperature changes, and heart rate variability (HRV), the variation in time between heartbeats. HRV usually drops when you’re stressed, sick, or haven’t recovered from hard training.The Google Health app uses those readings to set a Readiness score each morning. It also tracks Cardio Load, which estimates how much cardiovascular strain your workouts create, while your personalized weekly target helps you balance activity and recovery. It can help you spot changes in your training load, but it can’t tell you exactly what your body can handle. Both trackers can alert you to an irregular rhythm that could be atrial fibrillation. They can also notify you when your heart rate stays unusually high or low while you’re inactive. Both also have Smart Wake, which vibrates to wake you during light sleep inside a time window you set.The Edge adds a few health tools the Air doesn’t have. Its ECG app records your heart’s electrical activity whenever you start a reading. If your heart feels like it’s racing or skipping, you can take a reading in the moment and save it to show your doctor. The Edge has a dedicated skin-temperature sensor, while older Fitbits such as the Charge 6 use a device-temperature sensor to track overnight skin-temperature variation.With Google Health Premium, both trackers get Google’s advanced Health Guardian features, which track trends in your blood pressure and insulin resistance. Google says they aren’t meant to screen or diagnose any condition.Both trackers start logging common workouts on their own. In my testing, the Air logged walks and lifting sessions without my starting them. Google says an update expands automatic detection on both the Air and Edge from 10 workout types to more than 100, including strength training, swimming, and racket sports. A workout only gets logged automatically if it lasts at least 15 minutes and keeps your heart rate up, so you may have to log short or stop-and-start sessions yourself.

The Fitbit Edge has built-in GPS, so it can map your route and measure your pace and distance without your phone. Google says the Edge’s GPS is up to 40 percent more accurate than its earlier trackers, thanks to a new GPS chip and case design. The Edge also has an altimeter, which reads air pressure to measure how much elevation you gain on a hilly run or how many floors you climb on a stair workout.The Edge’s screen also shows your stats during a workout, giving you instant feedback. You can set a pace target before a run and check on the screen whether you’re ahead of pace or lagging behind. During HIIT intervals, you can see which heart rate zone you’re in. On the track, it shows your split for each lap.The Fitbit Air has no GPS and no screen. To map a run, you have to carry your phone, and you can’t check your pace or heart rate until you look at the Google Health app afterward. If you mostly lift or walk and don’t want instant feedback, the Air is a great option. But if you care about your splits, the Edge is the better tracker.

The Fitbit Edge comes with nine apps, including Google Maps, Weather, and Timer. You can’t download more, and unlike the Pixel Watch 5, it doesn’t let you talk to Gemini from your wrist. Google Maps shows turn-by-turn directions on the Edge only after you start navigation on your phone, so you can’t look up a destination on the tracker itself.Calls and texts from your phone show up on the Edge’s screen. On Android, you can answer a text with a preset reply like “on my way.” Those quick replies don’t work with an iPhone, so iPhone owners can read texts on the Edge but have to answer them on the phone. Swiping down on the Edge opens a control panel where you can turn on Do Not Disturb, use the screen as a flashlight, or make your phone ring when you can’t find it.The Fitbit Air has none of this. Its only feature you’ll notice day to day is the Smart Wake alarm, which vibrates to wake you up. Everything else, including the Health Coach, lives in the Google Health app, which also syncs with Apple Health if you want your data in one place on an iPhone.Neither tracker has NFC, so you can’t use either one to pay with Google Wallet.

You don’t need a subscription to use either tracker. Without one, the Google Health app still shows your steps, heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, sleep score and stages, Readiness, Cardio Load, and workouts. It also alerts you to an irregular heart rhythm. Google Health Premium costs $9.99 a month, and the Air and Edge each come with three months free.Premium adds the Gemini-powered Health Coach, which you can message anytime with questions about your data, plus weekly workout plans that adjust to your schedule. When I told it my shoulder was sore, it reworked that week’s plan around it. It also adds more detailed sleep summaries, meal logging from a photo, and plain-language summaries of your lab results.

The Charge 6 came out in 2023 and retails for $159.95. It has an ECG app and built-in GPS, and it can track more than 40 types of exercise. The Fitbit Edge improves on almost all of that. Its screen is 46 percent bigger, it’s rated IP68 for dust resistance, and it charges in about 90 minutes instead of two hours. And when the Edge’s battery wears out, you can replace it yourself instead of buying a new tracker.The Edge does drop two features the Charge 6 offers. The first is NFC, the chip that lets you pay with Google Wallet. The second is the EDA Scan app, which measures small changes in the sweat on your skin to estimate your stress level. If you’re buying a new tracker, the Charge 6 makes sense only if you pay with your wrist or find it well below the Edge’s $179 price (it’s down to $129.95 on Google’s site at the time of publication).The Fitbit Inspire 3 is the cheapest Fitbit with a screen, at about $100. It’s smaller than the Charge 6, lasts longer between charges, and starts tracking walks and runs automatically. It has no GPS or ECG, but it remains a solid choice if you want to see the time and your step count on your wrist without paying for the Edge.

Buy the Fitbit Air if you lift, walk, or take classes and mostly want to know how well you slept and how hard to train each day. At $99, it gets you the same heart rate, HRV, and sleep data as the Edge, and the same Health Coach if you pay for Premium. Because it has no screen, nothing on your wrist lights up or buzzes during dinner or in the middle of the night.For $80 more than the Air, the Edge gets you built-in GPS that maps your route and measures your pace without your phone. The screen shows your splits and heart rate zones while you’re moving, and the altimeter counts the elevation you climb. The ECG app also lets you check your heart rhythm the moment something feels off.If you already have a Charge 6, you don’t have to upgrade to get Google’s newest software. The Health Coach and Premium features come through the Google Health app, so they work on the tracker you already own. Upgrade to the Edge if the Charge 6’s battery no longer gets you through the week. But it’s worth keeping if you pay with your wrist. Neither new Fitbit has NFC, so the Charge 6 is the only one of the three that works with Google Wallet.

#4831. A Global Perspective on Youth Mental Health Decline

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

There is rather a lot going on at the moment, what with climate change, cost-of-living crises, geopolitical instability and so on. Not only has it been going on for quite some time, but also, the end of it does not seem to be nigh. And so, worldwide, it is affecting the mental health and wellbeing of many. However, it does seem to be hitting some a little more than others, especially those that aren’t as secure and positive about the outcomes of all these concerns or who have not yet weathered that many crises. In short, it appears to be disproportionately affecting the younger generations.

A recent survey of more than 50,000 people across 92 countries found that mental health is in decline. The word ‘languishing’ was used. In fact, authors called it a trend, and one that was disproportionately affecting younger populations, including in the wealthier countries. 1

To languish means to exist in a state of stagnation, weakness, or neglect. In psychology it often refers to a feeling of persistent emptiness and apathy, only without being clinically depressed. Basically, it means you’re really feeling really rather ‘meh’ about things.

The study, published in the journal Social Indicators Research, found that global mental health scores were being dragged down by the younger generations who lacked fundamental aspects of well-being, and reported lower rates of – among other things – vitality, emotional stability and resilience. 1

Kai Ruggeri, professor of health policy and management at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and lead author on the study said, “these findings are more than just a sign to policy makers that solutions are necessary to improve mental health among young people, or those struggling to make ends meet.”

In fact, he called the results a flashing red light that entire populations were already struggling, one that went beyond concerns for an uncertain future, and showed that resilience was being diminished in the here and now.

“Leaders can no longer use vague platitudes that hand-wave toward investing in non-specific mental health initiatives. They have to make specific commitments to significant actions: ensure livelihoods in the face of AI-driven job losses, address factors driving burnout in young working-age populations and take steps that will generate confidence toward future opportunities,” said Professor Ruggeri.

The survey was conducted mainly online and asked participants 10 questions about their mental health that captured data on feelings of competence, optimism, self-esteem, engagement, and vitality. It was then followed by questions and measurements concerning issues such as stress, depression, anxiety and overall life satisfaction.

The study found more positive signs amongst the older demographics. People who were employed and those who had higher incomes, perhaps unsurprisingly, also experienced better mental health and wellbeing outcomes.

Elsewhere in ‘youth’ another survey (this one national, American, and including more than 42 million participants) found that almost a fifth or adolescents and young adults aged 12 to 21 were using AI chatbots for mental health advice. 2

The study found that 42.8 percent of participants had consulted with chatbots on at least a monthly basis, and that 91.7 percent found them either ‘somewhat’ or ‘very’ helpful. And AI chatbot use was more frequent among females compared to males.

Reasons for use included accessibility, anonymity and the low cost. Another attractive feature was that they offered personalised and interactive guidance.

However, all this did come with a slightly worrying price attached as the authors noted that these exchanges occurred without oversight by adults and, especially, mental health professionals.

As AI therapy becomes more widespread amongst adults and young adults for both emotional and psychological support, the study authors highlighted a need for parents, clinicians and policymakers to understand their evolving role in youth mental health care.

When it comes to the latter study, I agree with the authors, it’s a wake-up call and things need to be done. If life (and by life, I mean society and all its constructs) is sucking the joy out of an entire generation before they’ve even got started, we seriously need to look at those constructs.

However, not everyone is as apathetic as the study suggests. It's not for nothing that Gen Z is protesting around the world right now. Just take a look at India, Serbia, and France. Some are calling the protests a global political awakening whilst others are complaining about them. Perhaps we need to listen more and move faster.

With the latter study, AI is here to stay (at least for now). The best we can do is advise caution and remind all those that use it that artificial intelligence gets it wrong. It makes mistakes. By all means use it but but cross-reference it and, when it comes to AI therapy, please cross-check with a trained professional.

1. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11205-026-03890-0

2. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapediatrics/fullarticle/2849307
